stories.body:
No breakthroughs on major subjects at first trilateral summit between leaders of US, China and Russia

T he presidents of the US, China and Russia met on Thursday for an unprecedented trilateral gathering on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen. The session lasted more than an hour and Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin touched on nuclear weapons, the war in Ukraine and wider international security.

The trio lead the world’s three major nuclear powers and their decisions have far-reaching consequences for global security. However, their meeting in China ended without an announced breakthrough or concrete agreement on the main issues. Here are five key takeaways:

Trump declared the meeting ‘historic’

Trump opened the talks by telling Xi and Putin that “we are really making history”. He described the US, China and Russia as “uniquely positioned” to discuss reducing their nuclear stockpiles and lowering the risk of such weapons being used.

It was an unusually high-profile display of cooperation between three countries whose relations have been marked by significant tensions, especially over Ukraine, trade disputes and the Nvidia scandal .

Trump also argued that peace could not be achieved by turning down opportunities for dialogue. It was the first time the leaders of the three countries had held a trilateral summit of this kind.

Nuclear arms control was a central issue

The talks came against the backdrop of the New Start nuclear agreement expiring in February . The treaty limits the arsenals of the US and Russia, capping each side at 1,550 deployed strategic nuclear warheads.

In September last year, Putin proposed voluntarily maintaining these limits for another year, but Trump rejected that approach, calling instead for a new agreement that would include China.

In the meeting on Thursday, Xi called for every effort to be made to prevent nuclear war and for nuclear weapons to be “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed”. However, no new arms control agreement was announced.

Ukraine was raised, without a breakthrough

Putin told Trump and Xi that their countries had “many converging interests” when it came to resolving conflicts, explicitly mentioning the war in Ukraine. He also spoke of their shared responsibility for international peace and security.

Like Putin, Trump arrived at the meeting fighting a failing war of choice. The Iran conflict has become an increasingly uncertain and costly undertaking for the US with no clear end in sight, while Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year, continues to exact a heavy toll.

The meeting offered little indication of progress toward ending the war in Ukraine, and Kyiv was not mentioned in the subsequent joint peace declaration.

Trump attacked the international criminal court

Trump described the international criminal court as “out of control”, criticising what he regards as the court’s excessive overreach.

His remarks carry particular significance given that Putin is wanted by the ICC on charges of war crimes. The court issued an arrest warrant for the Russian president in March 2023, accusing him of unlawfully deporting and transferring Ukrainian children from occupied territories to Russia.

The US and China are not signatories to the Rome statute, the international treaty that established the court, and are not bound by a requirement for member states to carry out its arrest warrants.

A joint ‘peace declaration’ was issued

A joint “peace declaration” issued after the meeting by Chinese and Russian state media called for UN reform “so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”.

The statement said the shake-up would range from boosting fuel supplies to engaging in “dialogue to reduce nuclear risks”.

The US and China are already permanent members of the UN security council, each with veto powers. They, and Russia, have argued for a greater role for nations from Asia, Africa and South America.

Russia has openly opposed permanent security council bids from Germany and Japan , arguing that western and Nato countries are already overrepresented and vote as a single bloc against Russian interests.

The declaration also took aim at the ICC, saying the court and similar bodies “must not abuse their jurisdiction”. It emphasised state consent and respect for the immunity of officials, which could be interpreted as a challenge to the legal basis for the ICC’s arrest warrant for Putin.

stories.title: Ted Cruz-led committee approves Trump FCC nominee 15-0 as Democrats boycott vote
stories.summary: Democrats try to prevent quorum, say Thumann lied about not working on media issues.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Democrats try to prevent quorum, say Thumann lied about not working on media issues.

A Senate committee chaired by Ted Cruz (R-Texas) voted today to approve a Federal Communications Commission nominee, despite accusations that the nominee gave false testimony about her work as a legal advisor for FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. Democrats attempted to prevent a quorum by not showing up, but Cruz proceeded with a Republican-only vote.

All 15 Republicans on the Senate Commerce Committee voted to approve Trump nominee Danielle Thumann, while the committee’s 13 Democrats were absent. “We’re going to be doing our job today, even if the Democrats refuse to show up to do theirs,” Cruz said at today’s hearing.

Nominees are vetted in committees first, and then require majority approval from the Senate. Republicans are hoping to get Thumann confirmed before Democrats take Senate control in January.

Although the Senate Commerce Committee generally requires one minority member to be present for nomination votes, a spokesperson for Cruz said Senate rules allow the nomination to be advanced for a vote in the entire chamber. A spokesperson for Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), the top Democrat on the committee, said in response that “since 2005, Commerce Committee rules required that a quorum include one member of the minority for official action on bill, resolution, or nomination.”

Technically, the committee has operated with no rules during Cruz’s chairmanship because Cruz “failed to pass committee rules” for the current session of Congress, Cantwell’s spokesperson said. “Nevertheless, in practice it has operated in line with rules from the last Congress (and this provision, specifically, since 2005), including that a quorum with a member of the minority party must be present for official action on a nomination or legislation. Until today.”

False testimony allegation

At a hearing last week, Thumann said she never worked with Carr on media-related topics, leading to accusations that she provided false testimony. “I have not worked with the chairman on any media-related issues,” Thumann said after Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) asked, “Do you support Chairman Carr’s illegal campaign to remove Jimmy Kimmel from the nation’s airwaves?”

“It appears that Ms. Thumann misled the Committee and offered false testimony, seriously calling into question her judgment and character and impeding the Committee’s work in determining whether she should be seated on the Commission,” Luján wrote in a letter to Cruz yesterday. “While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media-related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount.”

The FCC website describes Thumann as senior counsel to Carr on matters before the Wireline Bureau, the Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau, and the Consumer and Governmental Affairs Bureau. Emails obtained in a public records request by the group Protect Democracy show she had some involvement in media-related matters.

Thumann provided follow-up responses to senators’ questions this week. She said that her work sometimes includes “reviewing documents or filings in a matter outside of my designated portfolio. However, I did not have any conversations with Paramount, CBS, or Skydance related to the merger.”

Emails touched on 60 Minutes complaints

Thumann has been referred to as Thumann Severs in the nomination process, but she uses the name Thumann.

Luján wrote that Thumann “played a role in processing informal complaints related to” alleged news distortion on CBS’s 60 Minutes , and that “she apparently orchestrated the Commission’s response to consumers regarding the Jimmy Kimmel controversy.” However, Thumann was only a recipient of the Kimmel-related emails we found in a search of the messages.

The emails do show that Thumann approved language used in a response the FCC gave to complaints about the alleged news distortion in a 60 Minutes interview with Kamala Harris. The response informed people who submitted complaints that they should instead submit comments on an FCC docket that had been set up for the 60 Minutes proceeding.

“Hi Kristi, I have confirmed with the Chairman and Erin that we would like for complainants to be encouraged to resubmit their news distortion complaints in the relevant ECFS [Electronic Comment Filing System] proceeding,” Thumann wrote. “Can you please work on some draft language to send to consumers that would advise them on this step (including how to use ECFS)?”

Democrats aimed to prevent quorum

Democrats announced yesterday that they would try to prevent a quorum for today’s vote. They objected to adding a third Republican to the committee while a Democratic seat remains empty.

“All Democratic members of the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee object to the majority stacking independent commissions with Republicans and rushing nominees through the Committee process in this lame duck session with no Democratic pairs,” Cantwell said in a statement.

Cantwell and other Democrats on the committee sent a letter to Cruz urging him to cancel the vote, while quoting his own words from 2014. “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the Democratic committee members said.

Cruz said today that “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January. But today is November 18.” Cruz said there is “ample precedent” for advancing nominations in a lame-duck session.

Senate Commerce Committee rules state that a quorum for nomination votes requires a “majority of the members, which includes at least one minority member.” But a Cruz spokesperson pointed to certain clauses regarding committee quorums in Senate rules when contacted by Ars today.

In the Standing Rules of the Senate , paragraph 7 of rule XXVI says that “no measure or matter or recommendation shall be reported from any committee unless a majority of the committee were physically present,” and does not have any requirement for minority members to be present. Elsewhere, the Senate rules say that when a committee reports a measure to the Senate floor, “no point of order shall lie with respect to that measure” as long as the committee took its action “in conformity with the requirements of paragraph 7 of rule XXVI.”

While committees can have different quorum rules, a Cruz spokesperson said this functions as a “cleansing clause” so that “earlier procedural irregularities, such as a violation of a committee rule, cannot be used to invalidate the vote on the Senate floor.”

Cruz rejects paired nominations

FCC nominations have traditionally been paired with one Republican and one Democrat when there is an empty seat for each party. But Cruz said that’s not a requirement.

“There’s nothing that requires the president to nominate in pairs… the law merely says that no more than three of the commissioners may be from the same party,” Cruz said during the Republican-only meeting.

The Communications Act prohibits a single party from holding more FCC seats than is necessary to form a majority. It says, “The maximum number of commissioners who may be members of the same political party shall be a number equal to the least number of commissioners which constitutes a majority of the full membership of the Commission.”

Republicans would have a 3-1 majority on the FCC if Thumann is confirmed by the Senate. The sole Democrat, Anna Gomez, would have to leave at the end of 2027 if Trump does not nominate her for another term.

“There is no mandate for the outgoing majority to rush through a partisan FCC nomination in its final weeks… Ms. Thumann Severs’ nomination should be postponed until the next Congress and paired with Commissioner Gomez’s renomination and the nomination of an additional Democratic commissioner,” Democrats told Cruz in their letter this week.

stories.title: Elon Musk says record $446m spending on US midterms was 'pretty foolish'
stories.summary: The multi-billionaire also said he was "not Maga", distancing himself from the political movement linked to Trump.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 19 November 2026, 01:56 GMT

Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.

The Tesla and SpaceX chief executive was the election's top individual donor , giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.

Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.

Democrats won control of both chambers in the US Congress, flipping both swing seats and making historic gains in places that have for decades been controlled by Republicans.

The election was seen as a bruising defeat for Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living in the US.

Musk was speaking virtually , external at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.

"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.

He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."

This marks a major shift in tone by Musk, who has previously been seen wearing a Maga hat.

"I'm not just Maga, I'm dark, gothic Maga," he joked at a Trump rally in 2024.

Musk has worn a Maga hat in public on several occasions

For several months at the start of Trump's second term in the White House, Musk served as an unpaid "special government employee" and Senior Advisor to the President, leading the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) to cut government spending.

In October 2026, the Pentagon named Musk as a co-lead of a future of warfare study called Project Meridian, while he continued to travel with and advise Trump.

Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.

The large number of Republican losses could have implications for Musk and his businesses.

Democrats coming into power in both the Senate and House of Representatives have pledged greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the building of controversial data centres.

In Georgia, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the newly elected Democrat governor promised to limit the rollout of the massive buildings , as well as the tax breaks tech companies often get to build them.

Democratic lawmakers have also suggested that SpaceX, which has gained an estimated $10bn in new government contracts since Trump was re-elected, should be investigated.

Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election results

One of the most striking midterms wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas.

According to BBC analysis , Musk had spent at least $45m in support of Paxton.

Texas is where key operations for Musk's car company Tesla and rocket and technology firm SpaceX are based.

Musk said on Wednesday that he believes Texas' new governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, is "going to be quite moderate".

Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott, ending more than three decades of the party's control of the state.

The Tesla boss added : "I don't think she's a far-left governor. And based on everything I've heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor."

stories.body:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’

China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.

The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.

The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.

The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.

“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”

Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.

Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.

The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.

“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.

Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.

In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.

First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”

The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.

Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”

Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .

Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.

European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.

The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.

Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.

Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.

Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

stories.title: EU-UK talks going down to the wire, says No 10
stories.summary: The EU and UK are expected to reach new deals on food trade and visas for young people at a summit on Friday.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 19 November 2026, 14:17 GMT

Negotiations between the EU and UK are "going down to the wire" ahead of Friday's summit in Brussels, Downing Street has said.

The summit is aimed at reaching new agreements between the two sides on food trade rules, visas for young people and carbon emissions pricing.

Sources have told the BBC the UK is set to agree to a quota of 100,000 young people per year coming to the UK as part of a new youth mobility scheme.

Downing Street has not commented on the details, which would also allow young Britons to live in Europe.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions and debates" of the Brexit referendum.

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, she said she wanted to see easier trading with the EU, but added "not trade at any cost".

She also said the new deals could see UK companies having to follow EU rules, even those that do not trade with the bloc.

Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday evening, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from the deal on Friday.

"There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said.

"But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow.

"So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."

The prime minister's spokesman has said if a deal is secured, the government will introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes.

A new youth mobility scheme would aim to make it easier for young people to work and travel both in the EU and UK.

The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.

In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.

Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.

Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.

The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in the talks, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.

An agreement on trade could also remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the EU.

The government argues this could add £5bn to the economy and cut food prices.

However, it could mean the UK will have to follow certain EU rules on products, for example on gene-edited crops or labelling.

On immigration, Burnham has said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.

The prime minister has said the summit would allow the UK to raise concerns about the Made in Europe scheme, which is designed to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.

Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to building a closer long-term future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member - however, he has ruled out major changes before the next election.

The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU, the single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.

Earlier this week, former deputy prime minister David Lammy urged the prime minister to go into the next general election promising to rejoin the EU.

However, the subject has divided his cabinet with one minister warning of the costs that would come with reversing Brexit.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, speaking to The Sun , external , said he does "not believe for a minute" the country would "ever vote to rejoin" the EU.

He added: "I think what Burnham is doing is playing a very cynical political game. He's trying to pick up votes from the Lib Dems, pick up votes from the Greens, and using it as a massive distraction from all the problems that he can't deal with."

stories.title: Trump abandons his FDA nominee, and Senate scraps vote on his NSF pick
stories.summary: "This time requires leadership and fortitude," Senator Bill Cassidy said.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
“This time requires leadership and fortitude,” Senator Bill Cassidy said.

In the span of less than 24 hours, two Trump administration nominees have suffered sudden blows—Trump’s pick to lead the Food and Drug Administration and his pick to lead the National Science Foundation.

Late Tuesday evening, Axios reported that the White House had abruptly withdrawn its controversial nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the FDA. Overton, a top conservative domestic policy aide in the White House, has drawn criticism and skepticism from Republicans and Democrats alike over her stances on vaccines, abortion, vapes, and birth control. Overton opposes abortion—though perhaps not strongly enough for some Republicans—and supported Trump and Kennedy’s decried anti-vaccine policies and statements, vexing Democrats.

In her confirmation hearing in September, Overton consistently stonewalled senators on every topic, refusing to directly answer even softball questions from friendly Republicans, leaving lawmakers on both sides of the aisle openly frustrated. The questions she dodged included those on how she would handle the FDA’s current safety review of the abortion pill, mifepristone, which extensive data has established is extremely safe. She also wouldn’t say whether she agreed with Trump when he falsely claimed the measles vaccine is “quite lethal” or that children are given vaccine doses the “size of a soda bottle.” Overton repeatedly refused to answer whether Trump could ever be wrong.

Axios quoted a senior Trump administration official as saying that Overton’s nomination was dropped because she “lacks the support on the Hill to move forward with her confirmation.”

The Senate’s Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee, chaired by Bill Cassidy (R-La.), was scheduled to vote on Overton’s nomination Wednesday. In a social media post Tuesday night, after her nomination was withdrawn, Cassidy said he believed she had a “viable confirmation path.” But he said the nomination was “abandoned” after some anti-abortion senators sought commitments from her that they couldn’t get. “The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments,” Cassidy said.

“Unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats,” Cassidy noted.

O’Neill canceled

After Overton’s last-minute withdrawal, the HELP committee’s agenda for Wednesday was updated again this morning to scrap a scheduled vote on Jim O’Neill, who was Trump’s nominee to run the NSF.

O’Neill has been criticized for lacking the science experience needed to run the foundation. In the past, O’Neill worked as a Silicon Valley investor and entrepreneur and became a close ally of Peter Thiel. But under Trump, O’Neill has been the deputy secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services and served as acting director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. O’Neill took over the latter role after the former director, Susan Monarez, was ousted from it less than a month after her Senate confirmation. She later told Senators Kennedy fired her for refusing to blindly approve vaccine recommendations from his anti-vaccine advisors.

In remarks this morning , Cassidy said that O’Neill “did not do enough to stand up for science and against irresponsible decisions and statements from [Health] Secretary [Robert F.] Kennedy [Jr.].” As an example, Cassidy specifically referenced O’Neill’s role in the firing of Monarez. “Several members of the [HELP] committee had concerns regarding this,” Cassidy said.

“This time requires leadership and fortitude and standing up for what is right,” Cassidy added.

The NSF has been hard hit by the Trump administration and actions by Elon Musk’s DOGE. The NSF has been forced to cancel hundreds of research grants and taken brutal cuts to its budget and staff in the past two years. In April, the Trump administration also terminated all members of the board that steers the NSF, called the National Science Board. Former members feared that it would make way for O’Neill to stack the board with political allies, pointing to how Trump filled the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology with tech billionaires —including leaders of Meta, Google, Oracle, and Nvidia—instead of top scientists and researchers.

stories.body:
US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake

Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.

The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.

Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump , California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway .

White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.

“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.

“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.

Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.

Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep . Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.

Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.

“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.

Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.

“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News .

stories.title: Faults not fixed in 90% of homes in government insulation scheme
stories.summary: People who signed up to a government insulation scheme have been struggling to get their damaged homes repaired.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Ken Palfrey is among the home owners waiting for repairs to faulty insulation

Published 19 November 2026, 14:57 GMT

More than 90% of homes fitted with faulty insulation under energy-saving government schemes have not yet had repairs completed to fix the botched work, a minister has said.

The government found almost all homes that had external wall insulation installed as part of two of the government's ECO schemes had defects that needed repairing.

Speaking to a committee of MPs on Wednesday, Energy Minister Martin McClusky said repair works had been completed at 2,227 out of the 24,600 homes impacted.

He said he was shocked by the extent of the failures and has assured affected households they would not be asked to pay to sort out these problems.

McClusky told MPs the insulation schemes "didn't have correct oversight".

Ofgem oversees the ECO schemes and alongside TrustMark, a government-backed consumer protection service, is responsible for auditing homes to identify faulty installations.

The government and its partners have known about significant levels of defective and unsafe insulation for years, with audits finding poor work in October 2024.

Ken Palfrey, a 66-year-old retired builder from Birmingham, is among the home owners waiting for repairs.

He had external wall insulation installed through the ECO programme in 2024.

He claims the installation was "botched", causing damage to his window sills and leading to damp and mould on his walls.

He said he complained and after some months an inspection concluded the insulation had been fitted incorrectly and he was told it had to be removed immediately.

Palfrey said for two years he had been on a "merry-go-round", spending "hundreds and hundreds of hours writing emails and complaining to people".

Earlier this month, TrustMark referred his case to the National Energy Foundation (NEF), a charity that has funding from energy suppliers to put right damaged homes where the installer has gone out of business.

"It's been an absolute nightmare," Palfrey said.

"Every day of my life, every time you look at the insulation, you're worried about it."

A TrustMark spokesperson said it was working to contact affected households and to fix "the unacceptable problems left by this faulty external wall insulation scheme".

"We're sorry for what Mr Palfrey has been through and have referred him to the National Energy Foundation which should be able to get his insulation put right," the spokesperson said.

'Failures in the system'

Labour MP Bill Esterson, the chair of the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee, told the BBC he was seeking assurances that the victims "will be supported in a timely fashion".

But he said he was concerned that Ofgem, Great Britain's energy regulator, had "failed to identify whether work had been carried out or completed to a decent standard".

When asked if he had confidence in Ofgem at the committee, McClusky did not answer the question directly.

He said: "There's clearly been failures in the system. We're designing a system now."

He added Ofgem was a "very different organisation than it was a number of years ago".

A spokesperson for Ofgem said: "It is unacceptable that households have been left with substandard ECO4 work. Ofgem was not responsible for assuring the quality of installations."

The spokesperson said the Department of Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) "is responsible for the design and overall outcomes of ECO, and that Ofgem's role did not include assessing installation quality".

"Our role, set by government, is to administer the scheme and hold suppliers to account for meeting their obligations," the Ofgem spokesperson added.

"When serious quality problems emerged, we went beyond our core role to support affected households and help establish the scale of the problem."

The BBC has asked TrustMark for comment.

Ken Palfrey said his external home insulation was "botched"

The two ECO schemes that have caused widespread issues are known as ECO4 and Great British Insulation Scheme (GBIS).

ECO4 was launched in 2022 and since then, more than 300,000 homes have had heat pumps, solar panels and insulation fitted under the £4bn scheme. It is closing in December.

GBIS - which opened in 2023 and has now closed - was more narrowly designed to help households lower their energy bills by installing cheap insulation.

The BBC has been reporting on the impact of faulty insulation installed under these schemes in recent years.

Fuel Poverty Action, a campaign group, argues that problems with faulty upgrades under a range of government energy efficiency schemes could be affecting as many as 100,000 homes.

"Ignoring the other defective measures is shockingly negligent, and is causing huge harm," said Jonathan Bean, policy lead at Fuel Poverty Action.

"Defective internal wall insulation causes major hidden damage, making it a ticking time bomb in homes.

"The government estimates that 29% of it is defective but chose not to include it in the Find and Fix process."

A spokesperson for DESNZ said: "We inherited the failing ECO4 scheme, which we ended after it clearly let families down.

"No household should have to pay to put the issues right and TrustMark is working to support those affected to ensure this is the case.

"Our Warm Homes Plan will overhaul the system to protect consumers and ensure failings are not repeated."

stories.title: Outage Chaos: When Tech is too Big to Fail
stories.summary: Outages happen, but we deserve a resilient internet where no one outage at one company can put people at risk and disrupt the global economy. We can only get there by addressing an over-reliance on a few cloud monopolists through effective antitrust laws and interoperability requirements. Service outages, like we’ve seen recently at Microsoft , Apple *, banks , courts , airlines , and elsewhere, can be more than an annoying hurdle. Losing a vital service due to an error can cause the same impacts as a government-ordered internet shutdown—people losing access to vital information and lines of communication. As usual, the greatest harms are faced by people on the margins globally. There’s not much hope in companies out-nerding these issues either. Technical errors will always exist, whether it’s a bug , negligence from an administrator, or a malicious attack. The problem is an over-reliance on any one company or system when these inevitable outages occur. It’s a matter of public safety and economic stability that policymakers mitigate the impact of these disruptions before they occur. In order to do so, we must ensure antitrust prevents providers of key technical systems from becoming too big to fail. The harms inflicted by tech monopolies go beyond monetary costs to the end user. In fact, monopolists can often offer lower prices, or even offer free services, thanks to their greater scale and incentive to shut out competitors using free-flowing investment capital . The problem is this puts a few tech companies in a position of incredible influence. The true cost is a loss of control when our private data, access to knowledge, and free expression all become mediated by tools owned by a handful of billionaires. Losing diversity in our digital infrastructure creates a less stable and less resilient internet for everyone. This isn’t just a bad deal for us as individuals. Losing diversity in our digital infrastructure creates a less stable and less resilient internet for everyone. When everything from daily tasks to national security is reliant on a few digital monocultures , one mistake or exploit can cascade into an explosive impact. The risks multiply in the current investment climate, where financial markets reward companies that strip-mine redundancy and resiliency from critical systems. stories.title: Surveillance Isn't Safety: A Comic About Organizing Against Flock and Other Foes
stories.summary: In the new comic "Surveillance Isn't Safety"—available for free today— cartoonist Bryn Adams explores the growing movement against mass surveillance through their involvement in the community fight against Flock Safety in Cleveland, Ohio. It's a personal journey that will resonate widely with residents in hundreds of cities where communities are drawing the line against automated license plate readers (ALPRs). Jump to the Comic Or download the PDF Published in collaboration between EFF and Crucial Comix , Bryn's comic captures the authenticity of the grassroot backlash against the surveillance industry—undercutting Flock founder Garrett Langley's latest dubious defense that public opposition of his company's product isn't real. At the International Association of Chiefs of Police conference this fall, Langley accused the anti-surveillance activism of being driven by Russian bots and as being "inorganic." He pointed to the fact that many local groups were using similar language in their protest signs as supposed proof, when in reality, shared slogans are one of the hallmarks of a social movement. This was all misdirection from the grim realities that Flock and other ALPR systems facilitate: the mistakes are real; the abuse is real; the racism is real; and the targeting of dissenters , migrants , and abortion seekers is real. And, importantly, the cancelled contracts are real. Bryn's comic sheds light on the real abuses and threats driving communities to mobilize against Flock, Axon, and other ALPR vendors. It shows that coast-to-coast activism doesn't happen overnight—any more than a comic appears out of thin air as a finished product. As advisors on the cartoon, EFF watched how Bryn's script evolved from rough sketches to penciled drawings, then to inked and shaded panels, mirroring how the long-running movement against mass surveillance has steadily snowballed over the last few years. There is nothing “inorganic” about either: Both are built on passion, commitment, and putting in the work. Kristalina Georgieva says countries needed to be ready for tech rollout, adding: ‘You snooze, you lose’

Business live – latest updates

Booming demand for artificial intelligence will force the world’s most powerful central banks to raise interest rates, the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned.

Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the Washington-based fund, said demand for AI hardware and related technology products was pushing up consumer prices around the world.

She said that, alongside the energy shock from the war in the Middle East, this was adding to inflationary pressures around the globe.

“This calls for a tightening of monetary policy in many economies,” she said.

Speaking at the 2026 Apec summit in Shenzhen , Georgieva warned that both factors would push global inflation to 4.7% this year. She added that the rapid rollout of AI was also contributing to stronger than expected economic growth in several countries, despite the headwinds from the Iran war.

Central banks have been forced to raise interest rates this year after the outbreak of war in February drove the global oil price above $100 a barrel, reigniting inflationary pressures around the world. The European Central Bank (ECB) raised rates in June for the first time since 2023, followed by the US Federal Reserve in September and the Bank of England earlier this month .

Financial markets expect further increases in the cost of borrowing next year, as the rapid rollout of AI bolsters economic growth against the volatile backdrop of the conflict.

However, global oil prices have fallen back in recent weeks, following the US midterm elections and an upswing in the supply of crude . Fears about an AI bubble and febrile conditions in global equity markets could dent business investment, and economists warn of a slowdown in demand as high inflation squeezes households.

Georgieva said that while the energy shock would eventually dissipate, “AI is for ever” – making it a significant driver of world trade, competitiveness, productivity and economic growth.

AI hardware and related tech products now account for more than one-tenth of the world goods trade, a share that is rapidly rising, she said. But some countries were benefiting more from investment than others.

“To put it simply: you snooze, you lose,” she added. “Countries need digital infrastructure, labour markets and workers that are ready for AI, and risk mitigation – especially to control financial stability and cybersecurity risks.”

after newsletter promotion

Georgieva’s comments came a day after the ECB expressed concerns about the rising amount of debt that AI companies are taking on to fuel their growth.

The central bank said there were “historic parallels” with the dotcom bubble that led to a tech market crash at the turn of the millennium, as well as the sub-prime mortgage bubble that set off the 2008 financial crisis. It said in its financial stability review that any fallout from an AI crash “could lead to spillovers affecting euro-area financial stability”.

For now, at least, the sector is still booming. Thursday marked a pivotal day for AI as Anthropic debuted on the US stock market , raising the largest investment of any initial public offering after pricing at $83 per share.

The company, which makes the AI chatbot Claude, is expected to become one of the most valuable publicly traded businesses in the world at $1.5tn, despite reporting losses of $80bn in the first half of 2026.

stories.body:
About 2.6m adults are taking the drugs, fuelled by the regulator’s approval of the pill versions and a rise in male users

At least one person is taking weight-loss drugs in 8.5% of households in Great Britain, according to research, meaning there are more homes with GLP-1 users than those containing vegetarians and pescatarians combined.

About 2.6 million adults were using weight-loss medication in August, a rise of about 700,000 people since February, according to a survey by Worldpanel by Numerator .

In February 6.3% of households had someone using GLP-1 drugs, rising to 8.5% in August. Weight-loss pills such as Wegovy were approved in the UK in June. Patients previously had to use the injectable version.

Pills now account for more than one in 10 (11.2%) of GLP-1 users, while men are also driving the increase. Men make up just under a third (32%) of people taking weight-loss medication, up from 23% in February. Male users have nearly doubled to 830,000, up from 440,000 nine months ago.

The increased use of medications such as Mounjaro and Wegovy is causing people to buy less food at the supermarket and change their buying habits, according to a survey of more than 9,600 households.

In the year after starting to take the drugs, households with a GLP‑1 user collectively spent £1bn less on groceries than expected compared with similar households. In June, Worldpanel calculated the total saved by households with a GLP-1 user was £780m.

This represents 415m fewer items bought, or £389 a year displaced from the shopping baskets of households with a GLP-1 user, according to the research by Worldpanel, which has been tracking the effects of the drugs on buying behaviour since March 2024.

Nishita Pattni, a senior consultant for Worldpanel by Numerator, said: “In just six months, between February and August 2026, user numbers rose almost as much as they did in the whole of the previous year.

“For many people, a daily pill is far easier than an injection, and with the surge in male users, we only expect the appeal of these drugs to grow.”

GLP-1 users are now found in a similar percentage of households in Great Britain as those that buy popular branded products such as Kellogg’s Rice Krispies (8.6%) and Corona beer (8.4%).

People taking weight-loss medication were not simply buying fewer groceries, the research found. Spend and volume were falling at a similar rate, creating winners and losers.

after newsletter promotion

Products associated with indulgence, as well as impulse purchases, have taken the biggest hit.

Alcohol spend has fallen by 15% more among GLP-1 users than in households where no one uses GLP-1, while the spend on crisps has fallen by a similar percentage, as users tend to snack less.

Conversely, portion-controlled products are growing in popularity. There has been a 30% rise in the number of frozen ready-meals sold, and an increase in the volume and spend on hot chocolate and malt drinks as people who take weight-loss drugs continue to enjoy small treats.

Chantel Kennaugh, the head of public sector and nutrition for Worldpanel by Numerator, said estimates suggest that GLP-1 usage is likely to surpass 10% of households in Great Britain in 2027. “This is not a flash-in-the-pan trend, but a seismic change that requires retailers and manufacturers to rethink their strategies.”

stories.title: Crew unaware of risks before Mike Lynch's yacht Bayesian sank, say investigators
stories.summary: The vessel sank off the coast of northern Sicily, killing seven people including British tech tycoon Mike Lynch.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
There were 22 people on board the Bayesian at the time of the incident

Published 19 November 2026, 00:05 GMT

The crew of the Bayesian superyacht did not know about critical safety risks that left it vulnerable in powerful winds before it sank off the coast in northern Sicily, killing seven people, British investigators say.

British tech tycoon Mike Lynch, 59, and his daughter Hannah, 18, were among seven people who died when the vessel sank on 19 August 2024.

The sinking of the Bayesian unfolded with "extraordinary speed" when a violent downburst of freak hurricane-force winds knocked it onto its side in less than 15 seconds, the UK's Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) final report said.

Safety information provided to the crew did not identify this type of risk, the MAIB said.

"It was very dynamic, very quick," said MAIB principal inspector Simon Graves. "The speed of events overtook the crew and prevented them from taking any other action."

The accident also led to the deaths of Morgan Stanley International bank chairman Jonathan Bloomer, 70, and his wife, Judy, 71; American lawyer Chris Morvillo, 59, and his wife Neda Morvillo, 57; and crew member Rick Thomas , 59.

Mike Lynch and his daughter Hannah both died when the Bayesian sank

Rob Loder, chief inspector of marine accidents said: "Our thoughts remain with the families and loved ones of the seven who lost their lives, and with all those affected by the loss of Bayesian. This accident developed with extraordinary speed."

Fifteen survivors escaped from the 56-metre (184ft) luxury yacht and managed to get to a life raft that had been launched by a crew member.

The marine investigation found that the Bayesian "had a vulnerability to high winds that was not recognised, because the yacht had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down".

In addition, "the extreme winds that night were also not explicitly forecast, so the crew had no warning of the risk", Loder added.

WATCH: Millionaire Superyacht: Why Ships Sink

In the early hours of 19 August 2024 the Bayesian was anchored outside of Porticello port, on the north coast of Sicily.

With thunderstorms rapidly coming in, wind speeds went from 8 knots to about 70 knots (80mph) within minutes. The weather forecast had only predicted gusts of up to 27 knots (31mph).

The MAIB report stated that with no sails set Bayesian was vulnerable to being knocked over in severe winds.

It also found that any knockdown - where the boat was suddenly tipped sideways - would be "irrecoverable once the yacht passed the angle of vanishing stability", assessed in the study as being 73 degrees. Once the vessel passed this angle it could not right itself.

The wreckage of the Bayesian off the coast of Porticello, Sicily

In addition, the centreboard, which provides stability when a ship is under sail, was raised. The report said the centreboard was not needed when the Bayesian was using its motors and was rarely lowered at anchor. The way the boat was loaded, and the angle of the wind, also contributed to the accident.

Inspectors said a "downburst of hurricane-force winds" was the most likely cause of the ship keeling over.

They happen when cold, dense air plunges rapidly, sending out violent winds across the surface.

The MAIB said that none of risks were covered in the UK training syllabus, nor in published guidance available to crew.

Once the vessel was on its side, it rapidly filled with water and sank.

As it heeled over, five people were injured, either by falling or by items falling on them and a deckhand was thrown into the sea, the report said.

As water started entering the yacht, two of the guests "used the furniture drawers as an improvised ladder to exit into the central alleyway", then climbed along the internal walls to get into the saloon.

The MAIB's final report into the sinking, published on Thursday, appeared to contrast with recent reports from Italy, where prosecution experts have reportedly blamed errors by the crew rather than problems with the yacht.

The investigation was carried out alongside a criminal probe in Italy , where captain James Cutfield, chief engineer Tim Parker Eaton and deckhand Matthew Griffith are under investigation over potential charges of multiple manslaughter and culpable shipwreck.

British investigators said that Italian prosecutors had restricted access to some witnesses and evidence.

"It is possible that the circumstances depicted in this report may alter following disclosure of evidence withheld by the Italian authorities," the report says.

However, the MAIB's Graves said he was satisfied with the British investigation.

"We are content with our investigation, the investigation that we've undertaken, and the information we've used to feed into it."

The report also found that alcohol consumption had not contributed to the sinking.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

MAIB investigator Simon Graves: "This was an accident and there were a number of contributory factors"

The MAIB report makes seven recommendations to four agencies. It calls for new regulations to be set for single-hulled sailing vessels, and new rules around life rafts.

It also urges collaboration between the Met Office and its global counterpart to improve information-sharing of severe weather forecasts with mariners.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency is also investigating the sinking.

stories.summary: Simple changes at home can save pounds. Nanci Santos Iglesias/Shutterstock. As the weather turns colder and with energy bills predicted to rise, it’s the time of year when we look for ways to heat our homes more cost-effectively. Gas and electricity bills for a typical UK home are predicted to rise by 26% from January. Some financial support is promised by the government, including the household energy payment of £100 to many households in England and a VAT cut on electricity bills until July. In most cases, though, these measures will not offset the increase in bills, which is projected to be around £443 for a typical household. The UK has a high proportion of older properties , with 78% having been built before 1980. This means UK homes are often not as energy efficient as they could be, making them expensive to heat. Heat pumps, batteries, solar panels and full retrofit projects may ultimately reduce energy bills, but are expensive. As the weather turns colder and with energy bills predicted to rise, it’s the time of year when we look for ways to heat our homes more cost-effectively.

Gas and electricity bills for a typical UK home are predicted to rise by 26% from January. Some financial support is promised by the government, including the household energy payment of £100 to many households in England and a VAT cut on electricity bills until July. In most cases, though, these measures will not offset the increase in bills, which is projected to be around £443 for a typical household.

The UK has a high proportion of older properties , with 78% having been built before 1980. This means UK homes are often not as energy efficient as they could be, making them expensive to heat. Heat pumps, batteries, solar panels and full retrofit projects may ultimately reduce energy bills, but are expensive. Just 1.1% of homes in England and Wales reach an energy performance certificate score of A , and the vast majority (around 72%) score C or D, so there opportunities for all of us to improve our homes.

Reduce draughts

Draughts (cold air entering the house from outside, or entering a warm room from a colder one) dilute the warm air in the room with colder air, meaning our heating has to work harder to replace it. What’s more, draughts can make us feel cold even in a warm room, because air movement across our skin has a cooling effect.

The most common sources of draughts are windows, doors and letterboxes. Walking around your home on a cold or windy day will highlight any draughts. In many cases, draught-proofing can be a relatively cheap DIY job. Guidance from charity the Centre for Sustainable Energy explains how to go about it. A DIY draught excluder for the bottom of the door can be quite easy to make, and cut out some of the cold. A curtain behind the door is also effective, but make sure it’s wide enough to cover gaps around and below the door.

Energy advice charity the Energy Saving Trust suggests that professional window and door draught-proofing could save around £55 per year , and a chimney draught excluder could save another £45 per year.

Insulate

If the heat in our homes escapes, our heating has to replace it, which uses energy and costs money. Insulation stops this happening. Our homes should be insulated on all sides. This means the floor, walls, and roof.

In homes with a loft, this is often the easiest place to insulate. Loft insulation helps reduce heat loss through the roof. Insulating a loft now will reduce bills for years to come. This can be a DIY job, or can be done by a professional. Organisations such as the National Insulation Association can help find an installer.

If your loft is already insulated, you can add more insulation. The current minimum recommendation for new properties is 270mm, and increasing yours from 120mm to this level could save around £17-£20 per year . If you currently have less insulation, the saving will be much greater.

If you have a hot water cylinder, it’s also worth checking its insulation and adding or improving it. Insulating an uninsulated cylinder could save £200 .

In properties with single glazing, heat loss from windows will be large. While installing double glazing is a big job, long term benefits are large.

Heat to suit your home

It is sometimes suggested that leaving your heating on at a low level can lead to lower total energy use than turning it on and off. Whether or not this is true depends on your house, your heating, and you.

A detached house with thick stone walls will take a long time to become warm, but will stay warm for longer (this is also true in summer, and is the reason churches and old buildings remain cool in summer). A newer house with brick and plasterboard walls will heat up more quickly, but also loses heat more quickly.

It’s often better to maintain temperature in the thick walled older house, so here it might be better to adopt the “low and slow” method , particularly if you have a heat pump or a modern boiler. If you have a newer house, turning the heating on and off is likely to be the cheaper option in the long run. Using a smart meter, it’s possible to test both options for a week or so, then adopt the best option.

Not just heating

Heating is a major contributor to energy use, but it’s not the only one. Cooking, lighting, hot water and appliances all play a part. If you have any old-fashioned light bulbs, swapping them for LEDs immediately can save around £45-£55 a year . Using lids on pans, only boiling the water you need, turning off your oven and letting food finish cooking in the leftover heat, and avoiding the tumble dryer wherever possible are all good ways to save energy and money.

There are many other practical options, such as reflecting film behind your radiators, to reduce your energy bills without too much hard work. Just switching devices off standby could save £45 annually. Then of course there’s also looking at changing your energy supplier or making the most of cheaper electricity overnight. We haven’t included every option here, but energy advice services such as the Energy Saving Trust and charity the Fuelbank foundation can all help.

Bigger projects

If you’re considering a bigger project and want to really understand how your house loses heat and prepare yourself for the winter, there are charities and organisations across the UK who offer surveys, or may have infrared cameras available to borrow.

A survey will tell you where your house is losing heat so you can target your efforts in the right place. Some are available for free, and even if you’re not planning major work can provide useful information on cold spots and missing insulation. You could start with charity the National Energy Action .

stories.body:
Sleep-related infant death is an important public health concern . A recent review estimated the rate of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) in Africa to be among the highest in the world. According to the Global Burden of Disease study 2019 , the global SIDS rate was 20.98 deaths per 100,000 infants. Western sub-Saharan Africa had the highest rate at 41.80 per 100,000.

To reduce the risk of sleep related deaths, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that babies sleep on their backs, on a firm, flat surface, without soft bedding such as pillows and loose blankets. It recommends that babies sleep in the same room as their caregivers, but on a separate sleep surface. It also recommends that babies are breastfed.

Although not universally adopted, these recommendations are frequently cited in safe sleep research. Guidelines based on these recommendations were also recently used in a public health campaign in South Africa .

But this guidance may not always consider different cultural practices, family structures and living circumstances found in countries like South Africa. In the US, solitary infant sleep may be more prevalent, and living conditions are more uniform. In South Africa and other similar contexts, poverty, high inequality, crime and cultural beliefs mean a separate sleep surface is not always practical or desired. Caregivers may understand the recommendations but make different choices because of their babies’ needs, their own beliefs, or the practical demands of caring for a young child.

For example, in South Africa, bed-sharing (frequently called co-sleeping) is common. For many parents, having their baby sleep nearby makes practical and emotional sense. It can help parents monitor their babies and make night-time feeds quicker and easier . Caregivers may also have specific beliefs about how bed-sharing can promote parent-child attachment , or use sleep arrangements based on what works best for their household.

This creates a challenge for parents and healthcare professionals: how can infant sleep be made safer without overlooking the reasons families choose particular arrangements?

As a researcher and academic focusing on parenting and early childhood sleep, my recent study explored sleep practices and the motivations for using specific sleep arrangements among 201 South African caregivers of infants. An important part of the study was examining caregivers’ reasons for their sleep arrangements.

The findings suggest that promoting safer infant sleep requires more than communicating recommendations. It must also consider caregivers’ motivations and circumstances.

What does safer infant sleep look like?

The American Academy of Pediatrics’s recent guidance was developed in 2022 within the cultural and healthcare contexts of the US. These don’t necessarily reflect the realities of many other parts of the world.

Bed-sharing (a baby sleeping on the same surface as others) is a particular area of debate. It is not recommended by healthcare practitioners as it may increase the risk of sleep related death and accidental suffocation , particularly when other risk factors are present. These include soft bedding, sleeping on a sofa , and bed-sharing when a caregiver smokes or has consumed alcohol or other drugs or medication that cause drowsiness.

However, bed-sharing is common in many parts of the world, and some caregivers view it as a natural part of caring for their baby.

The recommendations provide an important foundation for safer sleep. But understanding how best to support South African families requires looking at what caregivers actually do and why.

What South African caregivers reported

Using an online cross-sectional design, I surveyed 201 caregivers of infants under one year about their sleep practices, their adherence to safe sleep recommendations, and their reasons for choosing particular arrangements.

The findings revealed a mixed picture. Most caregivers reported breastfeeding (85.5%) and room-sharing (90.5%). At the same time, bed-sharing was common (64.2%), and so was placing babies in positions other than on their backs (66.7%). Only 9.6% of caregivers met the criteria of placing their baby on their back and room-sharing without bed-sharing. These findings show why the recommendations need to be considered together rather than in isolation. Following only some practices does not necessarily mean a baby’s overall sleep environment is safe.

Caregivers gave different reasons for different sleeping arrangements. Feeding, bonding and safety were the main motivations for bed-sharing and room-sharing.

Feeding an infant often involves frequent night-time waking , particularly in early infancy. Keeping a baby in the same room or bed may make feeding more convenient.

Some caregivers also reported room- and bed-sharing as a way to bond with and protect their babies. This is important because an arrangement that a healthcare professional considers risky may be understood by a parent as a way of keeping their child safe.

Some respondents said their babies slept in a separate room, which is not recommended. Here caregiver sleep quality was a prominent consideration, suggesting that some caregivers choose this arrangement to improve their own sleep. This is relevant because caregivers also need sufficient sleep to function during the day.

Unemployment was associated with lower adherence to safe sleep recommendations, suggesting that adherence may partly be driven by household factors. Factors like financial strain and limited space may influence caregivers’ ability to follow recommendations. Bed-sharing for feeding or bonding may be common worldwide. But constraints linked to unemployment appear more context specific, and more common in countries with high income inequality.

What’s needed

Simply telling caregivers to use specific sleep arrangements may not be enough to change their behaviour. Advice that does not acknowledge caregivers’ experiences, beliefs and practical needs may be difficult to follow.

Advice that is appropriate for one household may not be equally feasible for another. Understanding these differences can help healthcare professionals move beyond general recommendations and have more useful conversations with caregivers.

If healthcare professionals, researchers, policymakers, communities and families want to improve infant sleep safety in South Africa, we need to combine clear information about risk with a realistic understanding of family life. It is an essential part of making that guidance meaningful and possible to follow.

Where a caregiver is struggling to avoid bed-sharing, it is especially important to discuss ways to reduce risk. Some countries such as the UK and Canada have begun to address this reality. For example, UK health officials advise healthcare professionals to discuss safer bed-sharing practices with parents.

South Africa needs to communicate recommendations in ways that acknowledge the realities of family life. Harm-reduction conversations should complement, not replace, advice about the safest sleep environment. This means recognising why caregivers make particular choices, explaining risks clearly, and helping families identify safer and feasible alternatives within their homes.
