stories.title: What China’s Gene-Editing Deaths Reveal About Its Biotech Industry
stories.summary: The post What China’s Gene-Editing Deaths Reveal About Its Biotech Industry appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Regulation alone won’t fix the conditions that have earned China the reputation of the “Wild East.”

Jane Qiu is an independent science writer in Beijing.

BEIJING — In March 2023, four-year-old Mei in Shanghai was diagnosed with a rare genetic mutation linked to developmental delay and autism-like traits. Although her condition was mild and she improved with therapy and special education, her parents remained worried about her future. Hopeful for a cure, they paid Qiu Zilong, a renowned neuroscientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and his team $860,000 to develop a customized gene therapy. The treatment, which used adeno-associated viruses to deliver gene editors to the brain, had been approved by Xinhua Hospital, a leading hospital for rare diseases.

On March 24, 2025, trillions of viral particles carrying gene editors were injected into Mei’s spinal cord. She soon developed a fever and kidney failure and died within days. A year later, Qiu’s team published its preclinical findings in Nature. Mei’s case was hailed by Chinese media as “a world-class breakthrough.” Mei’s death and her family’s financial support were not mentioned.

Deaths in clinical trials are not unusual. What is shocking are the regulatory lapses revealed by an investigation published this July in Science and subsequently corroborated by a separate investigation conducted by the Shanghai municipal government, which released its findings last week. The treatment’s consent form, for instance, didn’t warn of the possibility of death. The hospital had approved treatment before toxicology findings showing liver and kidney damage in monkeys that received similar treatments. And, among other crucial omissions, the researchers failed to disclose Mei’s death.

Apparently, this was not an isolated incident. Several researchers told me that Chinese hospitals commonly fail to disclose adverse events. On Aug. 5, STAT reported another death in a gene-editing trial led by Shanghai-based HuidaGene, an incident that had remained undisclosed for about 15 months. (The Chinese team published their findings , including the fatal case, in Cell on Oct. 26.) A founder of a rare-disease organization in China told me, on condition of anonymity for fear of political repercussions, that she had encountered other trials for genetic disorders in which deaths had gone unreported. Recent revelations of undisclosed deaths in clinical trials conducted in China have prompted warnings against the use of Chinese data in U.S. drug development.

As someone who has reported on China’s ethical governance for two decades, this all feels like déjà vu. Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies — that have earned the country a reputation as biotechnology’s “Wild East.”

Back in 2006, patients flocked to China to receive unproven stem-cell therapies . When immunotherapies came into vogue a decade later, bogus advertisements for unproven interventions proliferated online until the health ministry stepped in after the high-profile death of 21-year-old student Wei Zexi. Two years later, biophysicist He Jiankui shocked the world by announcing the birth of the first genetically modified babies created using CRISPR technology.

The response in China to Mei’s death has been divided. Some netizens portray Qiu as a reckless scientist willing to gamble with patients’ lives. Others, including longtime acquaintances, describe him as a diligent scientist committed to helping patients. In some respects, Qiu represents the antithesis of He. After the CRISPR-babies scandal, Qiu openly condemned He’s reckless behavior — only to become embroiled in a comparable scandal himself six years later.

It might be tempting to blame such scandals on individual failings. The deeper questions are: What systemic factors shaped their behavior? What does the incident reveal about China’s Achilles heel in biotechnology—and about the broader culture of international science in which it is embedded? And what can the lessons teach clinical research worldwide?

Fatal Flaw

It would be unfair to suggest that China hasn’t tried to strengthen its ethical governance. The CRISPR-babies scandal prompted deep soul-searching among Chinese scholars and government officials. Since then, President Xi Jinping reportedly championed an “ethics first” approach, contrasting the “science first” mindset often seen in Chinese research. New measures have included incorporating ethics provisions in China’s first Civil Law Code, creating a national ethics committee , and enacting new ethics-review guidelines for clinical research.

But powerful forces are also pushing in the opposite direction. In 2016, China launched Healthy China 2030, making rapid application of emerging medical technologies in clinical practice a priority — not only to address unmet medical needs but to boost national competitiveness. Reforms created a new pathway to translate basic research into clinical applications for cutting-edge technologies overseen by the health ministry, alongside the conventional drug-approval route regulated by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), China’s equivalent of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). This became widely known as the dual-track regulatory system.

“Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies.”

Under the technology track, clinical trials are often initiated by university researchers working with hospital clinicians rather than companies. Such investigator-initiated trials (IITs) exist worldwide. Until new regulations took effect this May, Chinese IITs were distinctive in that they could proceed with hospital approvals without the national regulatory oversight required for conventional drug trials. Compared with the NMPA route, the faster pathway allowed researchers to assess promising technologies in humans more quickly and at lower costs and help attract investment.

The result was a boom in IITs. By one estimate , more than 40,000 had been registered by April 2026, involving hundreds of thousands of participants and accounting for much of China’s translational research aimed at applying basic research to clinical practice.

China’s IIT model attracted worldwide attention. Kiran Musunuru, an expert on gene therapy at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, told me that “there is a widespread perception” that Chinese-style IITs offer a way to conduct first-in-human trials quickly and inexpensively. U.S. companies are increasingly interested in conducting IITs in China. Some U.S. researchers have even argued that the U.S should adopt elements of China’s model to accelerate drug discovery and enhance its competitiveness.

Critics, however, point to a fatal flaw: quality control. Driven by the pursuit of high-impact papers— whether for career advancement or hospital rankings — researchers rushed into first-in-human trials of emerging technologies. Hospitals are overwhelmed by proposals involving technologies with varying levels of risk. Researchers told me that as many as two dozen applications can be assessed in a single afternoon. In many cases, the process has become “a rubber-stamping exercise,” explained Zhu Wei, a bioethicist at the Shanghai Clinical Research Center.

A recent analysis of Chinese stem-cell IITs found that although a small fraction helped accelerate the application of basic research to clinical practice, most were repetitive, lacked innovation and wasted resources. Musunuru — who led the landmark development of a personalized gene-editing trial for Baby KJ, an infant with a rare life-threatening deficiency of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 that can cause dangerous ammonia buildup in the blood — warns that allowing individual hospitals to approve first-in-human trials of emerging technologies is particularly dangerous, because few researchers have sufficient experience to assess their risks. They would be “operating blind,” he told me, leaving the outcome dependent on “their appetite for risk.” That appetite can be amplified by institutional conflicts of interest. Successful trials of emerging technologies can bring researchers and hospitals fame, career advancement, high rankings and resources. Jing-Bao Nie, a bioethicist at the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand, told me that these incentives can undermine institutional judgment and jeopardize patient safety. In Mei’s case, he noted, the lure of a “world-class breakthrough” may have overwhelmed necessary caution. Political interference, which is common in China, is another way the appetite for risk may outweigh caution. Chinese researchers told me that senior hospital leaders often chair the committees that review trial applications. When they seek to push through major projects led by prominent scientists, other committee members may feel unable to object. Read Noema in print. A central regulator is more insulated from such pressures and can also draw on a far broader pool of expertise. As Musumuru notes, the FDA has an army of experienced reviewers who have assessed successful and failed trials, as well as those involving serious adverse effects. Its decisions are therefore informed by “the widest possible body of knowledge,” he told me. “That’s very reassuring.” Oversight Deficiencies Zhai Xiaomei, a bioethicist at the Peking Union Medical College and a member of the national science and technology ethics committee, was not wrong when she told New Beijing News that the problems exposed by Mei’s tragedy had improved since China’s State Council Order No. 818, which established a new regulatory framework for clinical research and commercial application of cutting-edge biomedical technologies, took effect this May. Under the new rules, only top-tier hospitals can undertake IITs. Trials involving emerging technologies like gene and cell therapy, brain-machine interfaces, transplantation and microbial therapies must undergo further review by the health ministry after hospital approval. Adverse effects must be reported within five working days. Violations can result in fines, suspension or permanent ban on clinical research, loss of licenses and even criminal charges. The scientific community in China and abroad welcomes the new rules. But a researcher working closely with the ministry, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to potential career repercussions, told me that it lacks sufficient staff with the necessary technical expertise to review the large volume of applications. Consequently, the researcher added, the reviews rely heavily on experts from universities and hospitals, with only a handful assessing each case. By contrast, Musunuru told me that the U.S. FDA employs numerous in-house reviewers, many with decades of experience, and dozens pore over each submission. If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, he argues, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality. “If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality.” More troublingly, Order 818 lacks mechanisms to monitor what happens locally and identify violations. It includes neither an inspection process — a crucial component of regulatory oversight in countries such as the U.S. and UK — nor a whistleblowing platform for reporting adverse effects and deaths. Such mechanisms are particularly important in countries where transparency is limited, and the press is not free. Without them, violations may go unnoticed and the penalties risk becoming little more than empty threats. Researchers, like bioethicist Ma Yonghui of Xiamen University, also worry that regulatory exemptions could create loopholes. Military hospitals, for instance, fall outside health ministry rules. The two dozen or so free trade zones across China, particularly in Bo’ao on the tropical island of Hainan, may enjoy special regulatory treatment, potentially attracting foreign researchers and companies seeking to conduct ethically contentious trials they could not undertake in their own countries. There are ample precedents of scientists exploiting countries with weak ethics governance as sites for risky research. In October 2018, one month before the CRISPR-babies scandal, He and John Zhang, founder and medical director of the New Hope Fertility Center in New York City, met Hainan’s vice governor to discuss establishing a clinic in Bo’ao to offer experimental procedures, including heritable genome editing. Zhang had already attracted international attention in 2016 for helping produce in Mexico the world’s first “three-parent baby” to prevent the transmission of mitochondrial DNA mutations from the mother. The procedure involved replacing faulty mitochondria with healthy ones from a female donor during in vitro fertilization, a procedure that was — and still is — illegal in the U.S. Hype & Hope While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations, Nie told me. The case offers a window into people’s relationship with biotechnology in China as well as their hopes and expectations — shaped not only by scientists but by society at large. Over the past decade, rare-disease advocacy organizations have grown rapidly in China, helping improve patient care, pressing for government support and driving research through collecting genetic data, studying disease progression and funding clinical trials. Su Yeyang, an independent anthropologist in Langfang in Hebei province who works with rare-disease communities, told me this has given families a sense of agency. With limited social support and a market-driven drug-discovery model that has failed rare-disease communities worldwide, they are doing whatever they can “to help themselves, their children and their community,” she said. With gene therapy, the “magic cure” long hoped for by many rare-disease patients seems within reach. In one high-profile case, a fledgling company approached Xu Wei, a high-school graduate in his 30s in Kunming, in China’s southern province of Yunnan, to develop a gene therapy for his son. The boy had Menkes syndrome, a rare genetic disorder that impairs copper absorption and causes developmental delays and premature death. The company, with no track record in neurodevelopmental diseases, claimed to have developed the treatment in less than a year. In 2022, the 3-year-old received it at a private hospital in a trial that, based on publicly available accounts, appeared not to include biomarker or behavioral assessments of efficacy. Chinese media reported enthusiastically on anecdotal claims of improvements while downplaying the risks of undertaking such experimental therapies. A patient advocacy leader told me such cases are not uncommon in China, where at least 20 million people are living with rare diseases. They offer hope, whether grounded in evidence or not, and can encourage others to follow. “We try to explain to families that pouring millions into a trial is no guarantee of success” and could even backfire, she says. Even well-educated parents, like Mei’s, may underestimate the complexity of clinical research and overestimate what experimental therapies can achieve. It’s unclear whether Qiu, who was fired by the university last week and barred from participating in scientific research for five years following the government investigation , helped foster such expectations. He has not publicly given his account. But his book, “ The Autism Enlightenment ,” published this April, was revealing. It recounted how, in 2010, he told the mother of a child with Rett syndrome — a rare, genetic neurodevelopmental disorder leading to severe cognitive and physical impairments — that a cure would likely emerge in three to five years. It did not discuss fatal risks often associated with first-in-human trials. It did not mention Jessie Gelsinger, who had a mild form of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, a condition that can lead to abnormally high levels of ammonia in the blood and died in 1999 from a preventable complication of an experimental gene therapy. “While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations.” Gelsinger was the first person publicly identified as having died in a gene therapy clinical trial, which undermined public trust in the field and set back its progress for decades. Nor did the book draw caution from the death in 2024 of a girl with Rett syndrome in the first brain-directed gene therapy for the condition. In both cases, scientists used the same type of virus as Qiu did. In a society where disability and genetic disease remain stigmatized, and families receive limited support, Mei’s parents placed their hopes in Qiu and gene editing. Like the couple who turned to He Jiankui to protect their children from HIV and the associated discrimination by editing their embryos, they sought a technological solution to social problems. As the Illness Challenge Foundation, a Beijing-based rare-disease advocacy organization, put it after Mei’s death , “responsible innovation should not entice patients to stake their lives in the name of hope.” China’s Gelsinger Moment? Gelsinger’s death in 1999 was a game changer. It’s widely regarded as a cautionary tale of how a toxic combination of scientific hype and insufficient safeguards can jeopardize patient safety. It triggered institutional reforms and significant changes in research culture in the U.S. that were aimed at rebuilding public and regulatory trust. Mei’s death could be China’s Gelsinger moment. It has exposed regulatory failings, a scientific ethos that encourages hype and recklessness, and deeper societal problems surrounding disability and genetic disease. None is unique to China, but they are particularly acute in a country facing a distinctive combination of political and developmental challenges. At the heart of the incident lies the “moral arbitrage” of experimental therapies, a recurrent theme in biotechnological innovation worldwide. On one hand, patients want access to cutting-edge, unproven treatments when they see them as their only hope. On the other hand, such treatments carry risks, which often accompany medical breakthroughs. Navigating the contours between hope and risk requires more than scientific evidence and regulatory rules, Su told me. It demands critical reflection on the culture of international science that places a premium on competition, sensational research, and being first at any cost. It also calls for broader societal dialogues about the diverse notions of human flourishing, the stigmatization of disabilities, and the need for greater support for people living with rare diseases. If China can learn from the failures and undertake the regulatory, scientific and social reforms needed to address its biotech governance failures — and if the rest of the world can look beyond the country’s small number of success stories out of a hidden ocean of low-quality and potentially harmful clinical trials — Mei’s death will not have been in vain. stories.title: Venezuela’s Base Deal Has No Voters
stories.summary: Venezuelans deserve democracy before, not after, a military deal with the United States. The post Venezuela’s Base Deal Has No Voters appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright speaks with Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodríguez during a press conference regarding the oil agreement reached by the US government and Venezuela on September 2, 2026 in Caracas, Venezuela. (Jesus Vargas/Getty Images)

In his first week as Venezuela’s foreign minister, Oliver Blanco sat down with Marco Rubio at the State Department on November 2. The official readout spoke of electoral reforms, political prisoners and the president’s three-phase plan : stabilization first, then economic recovery and reconciliation, and only then a democratic transition. It said nothing about soldiers.

A day later, The New York Times reported that the State Department, under Rubio, is negotiating a status of forces agreement with Caracas that would lay the foundation for a long-term American military presence. Troop numbers and locations would be settled in later agreements.

Washington will sell this as paperwork. The State Department says it has negotiated such pacts with more than 100 countries, which give American forces a predictable legal footing for ship visits, training, and exercises. Seen from outside Washington, Venezuela is not merely the latest entry on that list. It is a country whose president was seized by American troops on January 3 , whose interim leader holds no electoral mandate, and whose oil now carries a Pentagon stake.

A status of forces agreement signed under those conditions does not regulate a relationship between two sovereign governments. It writes a protectorate into law before the protected get a vote.

The soldiers, in fact, are arriving ahead of the lawyers. On October 30, Venezuelan drones and helicopters struck a Colombian National Liberation Army (ELN) camp in Apure state near the border with Colombia, and four U.S. officials told The Times that Washington supplied intelligence and drone support. The border rights group FundaRedes counted 23 victim s . Back in June, a Southern Command airstrike killed Héctor Rusthenford Guerrero Flores, a founder of Tren de Aragua, with CIA intelligence and Venezuelan forces taking part. After the June earthquakes, about 2,000 American troops moved into and around the country before pulling out again. The reopened U.S. embassy in Caracas already has a military attaché.

The readout leaves out an important motive for a future military base: the oil fields. In September, the administration announced a deal giving Washington a stake in about one-fifth of Venezuela’s oil resources. Caracas handed North American Blue Energy Partners, the vehicle of oilman Alejandro Betancourt, 100-year rights over 17 oilfields holding 65 billion barrels of proven reserves. The Pentagon owns 35 percent of that company, and Washington is guaranteed the right to buy a fifth of its output at cost.

Nobody leaves a century-long concession, part-owned by the Defense Department, without a guard. Donald Trump , speaking in Washington the same Monday Blanco visited, did not bother with euphemism. He referred to “our conquest of Venezuela.” Oil contracts are written for decades. So, it seems, are the garrisons that guard them.

Latin America has lived through this imbroglio before. In 1901, Cuba had to accept the Platt Amendment before American forces would leave, and the State Department’s historians list among its conditions the sale or lease of land for naval stations. The Guantánamo lease followed in February 1903. Washington repealed the amendment in 1934 and kept the lease, and the naval base still operates. The political tutelage was renegotiated. The military footprint signed during the tutelage outlived everyone who signed it.

The interim authority across the table from Rubio is in no position to bargain hard, and it has no mandate to bargain at all. Delcy Rodríguez has given no election date. Trump says Venezuela is not ready for elections. María Corina Machado, back after ten months in exile, wants a presidential vote by July. On Monday, teachers, nurses and university unions held a 12-hour national stoppage , demanding a $960 year-end payment that the government had left unanswered . The minimum monthly income stands at $240 . A government that cannot settle with its teachers is settling the legal status of foreign soldiers. Venezuelans can read that order of priorities. So can every capital in the hemisphere.

The counterargument deserves a fair hearing. Status of forces agreements are mundane instruments, and most of them govern exercises rather than occupations. The ELN and Tren de Aragua are real, and a Venezuelan army that sheltered guerrillas for years is now bombing them. The State Department insists that no base talks are under way.

But that is exactly the design of the deal. The framework comes first, and everything that matters (numbers, locations, duration) would be part of follow-on arrangements that neither an elected Venezuelan legislature nor the U.S. Senate will ever vote on.

The Democratic majorities that won both chambers on November 3 have three ways to keep this interim arrangement from hardening.

First, demand the text. State Department officials briefed some congressional aides on the talks in late October. A briefing for aides is not oversight.

Second, insist on the treaty form. Basing and status arrangements are usually concluded as executive agreements, not treaties. Venezuela is the case for the exception. An open-ended military presence in a country the United States attacked 10 months ago is the kind of commitment the Constitution leaves to two-thirds of the Senate.

Third, use the purse. A rider barring funds for any permanent presence in Venezuela until an elected government ratifies the arrangement would cost Washington nothing it needs this year. It would cost the oil concession its armed guarantee, and for obvious reasons the White House will fight it.

The timing gives the game away. If Rubio signs the agreement before the new Congress convenes in January, an outgoing majority and an unelected partner will have settled the matter between them, and Venezuelans will inherit the deal the way Cubans inherited Guantánamo. If the deal waits for a Senate vote and an elected government in Caracas, it may still go through. At least it will have voters behind it.

stories.title: Troubled Waters: Lake Victoria Faces an Ecological Reckoning
stories.summary: The largest tropical lake on Earth, Africa's Lake Victoria is under enormous strain, with its waters contaminated, fisheries decimated, and shorelines drowning. The losses have spurred renewed calls to protect the lake, which supports more than 45 million people across the region. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A Catholic priest offers a blessing on the shores of Lake Victoria. Priests perform rituals at landing sites, praying for bountiful catches at an increasingly unpredictable time.

PHOTO ESSAY

The largest tropical lake on Earth, Africa’s Lake Victoria is under enormous strain, with its waters contaminated, fisheries decimated, and shorelines drowning. The losses have spurred renewed calls to protect the lake, which supports more than 45 million people across the region.

By Matilde Gattoni and Matteo Fagotto • November 19, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

Lake Victoria, the largest tropical lake on Earth, is under enormous strain as overfishing, pollution, and a changing climate are decimating its fisheries, contaminating its waters, and bringing record floods to its shores. The losses have spurred renewed calls to protect the lake, whose basin supports more than 45 million people across the region.

For decades, Lake Victoria’s fishing industry relied on bountiful catches of Nile tilapia and Nile perch, both introduced to the lake in the 1950s. The perch, a voracious predator blamed for the disappearance of some 200 native cichlid species, became the lake’s most lucrative prize, with its filets exported to Europe and the Middle East. In recent years, overfishing has dramatically reduced fish stocks, including perch, pushing many fishermen to use illegal fine-mesh nets that catch juvenile fish before they can reproduce. Kenya’s catch fell from 94,349 metric tons in 2021 to 70,231 metric tons in 2025, according to the country’s fisheries service. In Uganda, the number of plants processing Nile perch has dropped from 21 to six, according to the director of operations at Victoria Treasures, one of the few surviving factories.

Pollution from farms, gold mining, and booming shoreline cities — including Kampala, Uganda’s capital, and Mwanza, Tanzania’s second-largest city — has compounded the damage as untreated sewage and fertilizers feed recurring algal blooms and water hyacinth invasions, which starve the water of oxygen and suffocate fish.

Yale Environment 360 / Created with Datawrapper

Making matters worse, exceptional rains linked with climate change lifted the lake to record levels in 2020 and again in 2024. The floods have forced hundreds of thousands of people from their homes and swallowed farmland and fish landing sites. The World Meteorological Organization expects this year’s El Niño, which typically brings heavier rains to East Africa, to last into 2027, raising the risk of further displacement.

In July, during the UNESCO World Heritage Committee meeting in Busan, South Korea, more than 100 civil society groups from 35 countries proposed recognizing Lake Victoria as a living cultural landscape, based on the fishing knowledge, rituals, and oral traditions its lakeside communities have accumulated over generations. The groups insisted that any nomination should protect local communities from displacement and safeguard the livelihoods of both fishers and the women who sell their catch.

If approved, inscription on the World Heritage list could bring international attention, technical help, and limited funding. It would also commit the governments of Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania to protecting the lake under an agreed management plan.

Photographer Matilde Gattoni spent February and March on Lake Victoria’s Kenyan, Ugandan, and Tanzanian shores. This photo essay combines images that reflect the lake’s dire condition — from the water hyacinths that clog landing sites to the residents displaced by floods — with images that speak to the countless ties, both economic and spiritual, that continue to bind the people to the lake.

Scroll down to see the images, or click on the photo below to launch a slideshow.

Invasive water hyacinth in Ogenya, Kenya, robs the lake of dissolved oxygen and blocks sunlight from penetrating the water. The weed, pushed by the wind into shallow areas, also keeps fishermen from reaching open water.

In Sindo, Kenya, women working as fishmongers vie for a piece of a dwindling catch. The competition has led to jaboya , or “sex for fish”: Women must trade sexual favors with fishermen to secure enough product to provide for their families.

Joyce Akinyi Odiko, 53, began as a fish seller but eventually assembled her own fleet of 30 boats, becoming one of the few women on the lake to own what she catches. As fisheries collapse in Uhanya, Kenya, she is considering selling her boats and leaving fishing behind.

A trader sells omena and fried fish in the largest market in Kisumu, Kenya. Populations of omena have plummeted as a result of overfishing and warming that is reducing oxygen levels in the lake.

A young woman in Uhanya, Kenya, wades through the submerged ruins of a communal fish processing site. In many coastal villages, floods have swallowed infrastructure, displaced residents, and moved the shoreline hundreds of feet inland.

Rising lake levels destroyed the mud and log home of Jane Anyango Okelo, in Ogenya. When the water receded it left behind highly fertile soil for crops, but Jane and her husband can’t afford to rebuild their home and now live in a makeshift tent.

A girl eats her only meal of the day in an alley of the informal camp at the Kigungu landing site in Uganda. Most of the people here are refugees from Makusa and Lwamunyo islands, which were almost entirely submerged by floods in 2020.

Many fishermen have turned to sand mining in nearby river mouths as fish stocks have shrunk. The practice is illegal as dredging destroys vital fish breeding grounds, disturbs the habitats of hippos and crocodiles, and leads to the erosion of wetlands.

A laborer carries a massive bundle of rice hay on his back after the harvest in Nduru, Kenya. Fertilizer runoff from farms in the region flows directly into the nearby Nyando River and into Lake Victoria, fueling the growth of invasive water hyacinth that chokes the shoreline.

Mercury used in informal and largely unregulated gold mining operations in Macalder, Kenya, can spill into rivers that eventually discharge into Lake Victoria.

A young girl in Kigungu examines a freshly caught Nile perch. Stocks of the highly profitable fish have dwindled, so processing companies now hire agents to scour landing sites and rush large specimens to factories for export.

stories.title: The End Of Extraction
stories.summary: The post The End Of Extraction appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Synthetic substances replacing extractive industries is a tale as old as capitalism. But frontier technologies are poised to accelerate that process, which can cause major disruptions to local communities.

Benjamin Siegel is a professor of history at Boston University and the author of “Markets of Pain: Opium, Capitalism, and the Global History of Painkillers.” He is currently writing a global history of protein for Ecco.

In the middle of Norway’s Hardangerfjord, I steady myself against waves that jostle the floating metal ring that encircles an enormous fish pen. My burly host laughs as I grip the railing. He needs no such assistance. With one hand, he grips an oversized bucket of pellets; with the other, he launches a spray into the pen. The water ripples and an instant later a silvery-blue cloud of salmon bodies starts breaking the surface.

This little meal is just for show. Throughout the day, a giant Akvasmart feed system shoots an enormous cascade of pellets — a mix of grains, legumes, synthetic astaxanthin pigment and the cooked, pressed and processed bodies of smaller, scaly fish — through long pipes into the pen, where between 150,000 and 200,000 salmon are growing plump. Across all the pens of the facility, more than a million salmon are raised this way.

Not long before visiting Hardangerfjord, I was walking down a long dock in Chimbote, Peru. Usually, one of the sprawling plants behind me would have been belching out fumes, processing anchoveta — a small, oily fish caught in enormous quantities off the South American coast — into protein-rich fishmeal for farmed fish and livestock, and into oil prized for its omega-3s. But fishing had been temporarily suspended to protect the stock as El Niño warmed the waters off Peru, and only the faintest smell of fish and sewage wafted across the bay. Everyone was frustrated, from the fishermen lingering in the port town to the factory managers who would otherwise be overseeing the processing of billions of finger-length fish by shiny German-made machines.

The fishmeal industry, like many other extractive ones, is resilient and adaptive. It was born of scrappy ingenuity in the 1950s, when local businessmen repurposed old tuna canneries and sold fishmeal to postwar European and American farmers to fatten chickens and hogs. It crashed dramatically in the early 1970s as overfishing and a powerful El Niño devastated anchoveta stocks, then was born again in the 1990s as global aquaculture expanded — especially Norway’s new salmon industry. Today, executives in Lima told me, Chinese demand for grouper and crab feed keeps their industry hot, with some modest help from the Americans and Europeans who purchase fish oil supplements in abundance.

But the same ingenuity that built the fishmeal industry stands to transform it beyond recognition. Just as Norwegian and Chilean salmon producers learned to use less fishmeal by substituting plant proteins, the Chinese aquaculture industry will be quick to replicate the same industrial sleight of hand. Fish oil, the other valuable product extracted from those billions of tiny fish, is contending with substitutes of its own. Feed companies can already obtain prized fatty acids, used in both omega-3 supplements for humans and in feed for farmed salmon, from algae grown in fermentation tanks and from canola bioengineered to produce them. For now, these substitutes remain expensive and difficult to scale. But if they become cheap enough to absorb the growth in demand, aquaculture could grow increasingly independent of the anchoveta catch it once depended on.

It’s a story as old as capitalism. A substance essential to modern life is grown or mined for a time, sustaining jobs (albeit often coercive, poorly paid, dangerous ones) and underpinning supply chains, but before long, a technoscientific innovation replicates that commodity or its function in a laboratory. Sometimes that ersatz substance is made from other, less geographically particular resources: tree resins, field crops, petroleum. Eventually, the supply chain migrates away from the original resource, stranding people and economies. The commodity may persist, or even thrive as a premium good, while losing the scale, price and indispensability that once sustained places organized around its production. Nylon took the place of silk in stockings and parachutes, polypropylene displaced sisal in agricultural twine, and synthetic opioids such as fentanyl allowed drugmakers to produce powerful painkillers without growing a single poppy.

“The production of critical materials — and with it some limited bargaining power — is moving from fields and cultivators toward firms controlling datasets, patents and bioreactors.”

This pattern is about to become easier to repeat. Protein language models can explore vast regions of protein sequence space, synthetic biology can program microbes to produce particular compounds and precision fermentation offers one way to produce them at industrial scale. SpudCell , an experimental synthetic cell announced in July 2026 by teams at the University of Minnesota, hints at more radical biological transformations to come. Assembled from nonliving components, it can grow, copy its DNA and divide itself independently. Finding useful substitutes has long been a sluggish, episodic process, but tools like these may make the search more systematic, expanding the range of resources whose uses can be replicated at industrial scale.

We do not need to know the year when tank-fermented omega-3s become cheap enough to displace fish oil in order to start counting the people whose livelihoods may melt into air. Elsewhere in the food industry, egg and whey proteins made by genetically engineered microbes have already entered the market. Firms are developing substitutes for coffee and cocoa — on which millions of smallholder farmers and their families depend — using other crops, by-products and processes to reproduce their flavors, fats and functional compounds. Substitutes don’t need to perfectly replicate a coffee bean or cacao pod, much less eliminate its cultivation, to erode the markets that sustain those producers.

The production of critical materials — and with it some limited bargaining power — is moving from fields and cultivators toward firms controlling datasets, patents and bioreactors. These technologies promise real emancipations. They might lessen pressure on fragile ecologies, loosen the links between consumption and forced labor, and insulate food supplies from the vagaries of climate and disease. But for regions overly dependent on a single commodity, the same progress carries the prospect of ruin.

The transition away from resource extraction will require a “temporary phase of maladjustment” every bit as tumultuous as the technologically driven unemployment that John Maynard Keynes described a century ago. But some transitions will merit anticipation and management, particularly when their benefits are widely dispersed while their costs are concentrated in places with little capacity to absorb them.

In Botswana , an extractive development model turned diamonds into schools, hospitals and the infrastructure of an upper-middle-income state. Competition from laboratory-grown stones, alongside weakening demand for mined diamonds, is already unsettling the fiscal foundations of that achievement. Malawi remains heavily dependent on burley tobacco exports. Nicotine in e-cigarettes and pouches can be extracted from tobacco scraps, weakening the case for paying for the qualities that make cured leaf valuable to cigarette manufacturers. Nicotine, too, can be synthesized without the plant. If smokers continue migrating toward these products, demand for nicotine could outlast demand for Malawi’s leaf.

What happens to Malawi’s tobacco growers when it does? Beyond the specter of existential risk, much of the hand-wringing over artificial intelligence turns on what will become of knowledge workers when a machine can do their work. Cultivators, miners and fishermen around the world will confront a question familiar to generations of others who cultivated or extracted some natural resource for a global trade: What happens when chemists learn to make that resource in a distant lab?

Madder is a compact, leafy cousin of the coffee plant. It shoots its slender roots deep into loamy soil. Dried and ground, those roots yield a red dye of inimitable richness. Madder colored textiles buried with Tutankhamun and the russet horses of the Bayeux Tapestry; transformed into a translucent pigment, it gave warmth to garments painted by Raphael, Rembrandt and Vermeer. Its reds became emblems of national identity, from the coats of British infantrymen and Ottoman fezes to the red-and-white bandanas of the American cowboy.

But in 1868, two German chemists, Carl Graebe and Carl Liebermann, coaxed alizarin, one of madder’s red colorants, from a compound found in coal tar. A cheaper industrial process followed the next year. As production expanded, madder growers from Holland to the south of France to the Levant found that buyers purchased far fewer of the roots that they had once meticulously shade-dried and powdered.

In the decades after, the world’s riot of natural color gave way to sophisticated distillations of hydrocarbons synthesized in the German and Swiss cauldrons of capitalism. Peasants in Oaxaca, Guatemala and the Canary Islands were next to learn that the cochineal insects they bred on prickly-pear cactuses and rendered into dye lost most of their textile market to chemical substitutes. In eastern India, synthetic blues doomed the natural indigo that European planters had forced peasants to cultivate.

Two years after Graebe and Liebermann’s 1868 synthesis of alizarin, the American inventor John Wesley Hyatt , working to produce billiard balls without the expense of ivory, patented a process for turning nitrocellulose and camphor into the world’s first commercially successful plastic. Celluloid promised to loosen manufacturing’s dependence on rare animal materials, even as it created new demands on natural camphor forests. “As petroleum came to the relief of the whale,” an 1878 pamphlet crowed, so “has celluloid given the elephant, the tortoise, and the coral insect a respite in their native haunts; and it will no longer be necessary to ransack the earth in pursuit of substances which are constantly growing scarcer.” This prediction was premature. But by the closing decades of the 19th century, these ersatz products were bringing creature comforts to the masses.

BASF drove several early severances. The company made good on the chemical fantasy of the early 19th century — no less a dream, the theorist Esther Leslie wrote, than “to reproduce the world synthetically and from the cheapest stuffs.” BASF scientists were farsighted in their vision of remaking the foundations of life itself.

One of the great infusions of soil fertility came from Peru, where workers mined millions of tons of nitrogen-rich guano from coastal islands. As the richest deposits were exhausted, Chilean nitrate took its place. Then the Haber-Bosch process , commercialized by BASF, displaced nitrate with ammonia made from atmospheric nitrogen, helping drive the long decline of Chile’s nitrate export economy — but enabling a great global growth in agricultural productivity that today sustains half the world’s population.

Substitutes derived from tree resins and fossil fuels cleaved a range of industries from their former natural suppliers. Japan’s colonial camphor monopoly in Taiwan had turned mountain trees into celluloid, photographic film, explosives and moth repellents before a German firm turned turpentine into a synthetic equivalent. At roughly the same time, chemists learned to dissolve wood pulp and respin its cellulose into rayon. “At last,” the American scientific evangelist Edwin Slosson exulted in 1919, “man has risen to the level of the worm and can spin threads to suit himself.”

“No government or institution has yet built a transition mechanism directly linking the rise of a laboratory-developed substitute to the restructuring of the region whose commodity it displaces. But many of the necessary frameworks already exist.”

Slosson, like many futurists of his age, saw in silk an inevitable law of development that governed the world’s natural resources: Man would use natural products, learn to cultivate them and eventually manufacture substitutes. That logic was cold comfort to the women in Japan who had grown mulberries and raised silkworms for American and European hosiery, and who watched rayon and then nylon decimate their production. Bengal’s jute cultivators supplied the raw material for sacks and hessian, and on Tanganyika’s sisal plantations, workers stripped leaves into fiber for twine and rope. Petroleum-based substitutes ate steadily into both markets. Read Noema in print.

The very goal of science, the British polymath J.B.S. Haldane predicted in 1923, was “man’s gradual conquest, first of space and time, then of matter as such, then of his own body and those of other living beings.” This conquest soon reached medicines and insecticides. After World War II, synthetic antimalarials sharply reduced the market for quinine from Java’s cinchona plantations; synthetic insecticides later came for Kenya’s pyrethrum trade.

Soon the conquest came for reproduction. Beginning in the 1940s, chemists at Mexico-based pharmaceutical firms turned diosgenin from wild barbasco yams into inexpensive steroid hormones, including progesterone and the progestins that helped make the birth-control pill possible. The trade boomed for three decades, but from the 1970s, microbial processes using soy sterols, total chemical synthesis and cheaper Chinese yams steadily displaced barbasco harvested in Veracruz, Oaxaca and Tabasco.

Many 20th-century substitutions, when they did not initiate a geographically concentrated shock, appeared to be unalloyed progress. The invention and commercialization of recombinant human insulin in the late 20th century meant that Eli Lilly and Novo Industri — later Novo Nordisk — no longer needed pig and cow pancreases. And some severances were less than absolute. Bangladeshi and Tanzanian farmers continued to grow jute and sisal long after they lost their commercial luster; a much-diminished Peruvian industry to this day exports cochineal to tint certain shades of Maybelline lipstick, Yoplait strawberry yogurt and Theraflu cold and cough caplets.

Political protection can keep systems operating and crops growing for decades, allowing entire systems of dependence to grow around them. In 2019 in Mandsaur, a flat and hot district in India’s historic opium heartland, I walked compact poppy fields where parchment-white flowers were dropping off knobby capsules. A few weeks after my winter visit, the men and women I spoke with would score those poppies with curved knives, harvesting raw opium sap in a manner unchanged for two centuries.

The crop still underwrites domestic painkiller production in India. But although there is no meaningful economic or pharmaceutical case for harvesting it by hand, the farmers’ votes have kept fieldhands busy. Beginning in the 19th century, advances in chemistry and pharmacology threatened to sideline the opium poppy’s role in pain relief. Poppies continued to be grown by smallholders in India and Turkey, under regimes structured by treaty and policed by a global bureaucracy — until a re-engineered Tasmanian poppy and synthetics like fentanyl reduced the role of the farmer, the plant and the field in the work of pain relief. Even those Tasmanian poppies may not last: Researchers have also produced opioid compounds in engineered yeast, opening the possibility of future severances.

Keeping India’s opium harvest going carried costs of its own. A crop turned just as easily into heroin as into morphine fueled a regional black market. Farmers were encouraged to keep planting, delaying the transition to other crops or other work. Ending the harvest grew harder with each season: It meant replacing livelihoods, unwinding electoral bargains and disrupting illicit supply chains that decades of protection had helped entrench. For regions facing the next wave of substitutes, the question is how to begin financing other livelihoods while the old industry still sustains them.

No government or institution has yet built a transition mechanism directly linking the rise of a laboratory-developed substitute to the restructuring of the region whose commodity it displaces. But many of the necessary frameworks already exist.

Fifty years ago, governments understood that eliminating a crop would require compensating farmers to leave it behind, though they struggled to dislodge regionally important crops. Turkey’s 1971 poppy ban , an early salvo in the U.S. “war on drugs,” failed to make good on its promise of a well-compensated transition away from opium into crops like lentils or beets.

Later and better-organized efforts in the Global North with the weight of large industries behind them fared better. In 2006, when the European Union shrank its sugar industry, it created a restructuring fund that ultimately took in about €6.2 billion. A levy on quota holders financed factory closures, paid growers and helped diversify the hardest-hit regions; the EU supported 18 African, Caribbean and Pacific sugar economies as the preferential market on which they had long depended was reorganized.

In that same decade, America’s tobacco buyout required manufacturers and importers to finance payments to growers and quota owners. That model was basic but portable: Peru adopted a version of it in 2008 when its fishing industry sought to end the wild scramble for anchoveta. The fishing companies that retained lucrative quota rights were required to finance retraining, retirement and small-business assistance. In Chimbote, I spoke with many fishermen still bristling at being pushed aside, but the compensation model is one foundational framework.

A second approach begins with the idea that industries owe a share of the wealth they create to the people and places that supplied their biological resources and knowledge. Efforts to put that obligation into practice gained ground in the early 21st century, but the promised benefits have generally failed to materialize.

After public pressure, South Africa’s national research organization agreed to share with the San people royalties from an appetite-suppressing compound derived from hoodia , a spiny desert succulent. UC Berkeley and the AIDS Research Alliance made similar agreements with the Samoan government and descendants of traditional healers over an antiviral compound isolated from the mamala tree. Neither compound was ever commercialized. South Africa’s rooibos industry offers a rare example of payments that did reach communities: It now pays the Khoikhoi and San, recognized as the plant’s traditional knowledge holders, a small levy tied to the crop’s farm-gate price.

International law and agreements have offered conceptual frameworks for sharing. The Nagoya Protocol , adopted in 2010, strengthened international rules for sharing the benefits of genetic resources with the countries and communities that provide them. The Cali Fund, which took shape at the 2024 and 2025 COP16 sessions, asks companies profiting from genetic-sequence data to share some of that value with biodiversity-rich countries and communities. But these schemes have outpaced countries’ and companies’ willingness to adopt them: The Nagoya Protocol has yet to be meaningfully implemented, and as of October 2026, the Cali Fund had received just over $10,000 from five contributors. And a focus on genetic data does little for the commodity markets that laboratory substitutes will disrupt.

“Chemists have been removing place from product since they first learned to make madder red from coal tar. Emerging technologies could bring that upheaval to more places in quicker succession.”

But the case for financing transitions should appeal more directly to consuming countries’ own self-interest. Perhaps the bluntest consequence of uncompensated severances is that they would undermine their own environmental promise, sending a cocoa or coffee farmer into forest clearing or illegal mining. The costs could spread through political instability and migration, import bans and tariffs, and subsidies that keep declining industries alive. (Just ask a director in India’s labyrinthine opium bureaucracy.) A collapse in Botswana’s diamond market could threaten healthcare in Gaborone and Francistown, while rising debt and falling demand would carry the shock across Southern Africa and beyond. Displacement from coffee- and cocoa-growing regions could likewise reshape politics in the Global North.

Converting foreknowledge into leverage is a global project, and no national or regional scheme will be large enough. But the European Union has the regulatory influence on supply chains to start it. Already, the EU makes importers of certain steel products account for the carbon dioxide emitted in making them. From the end of 2026, operators selling products like coffee, soy and cocoa in the EU will have to demonstrate that these products are deforestation-free. Already, these regulations are proving more consequential than their detractors believed. This October, in Mato Grosso, Brazil, I spoke with a soy farmer in front of a vast field of seedlings, listening as he described how planters and processors were working to meet this new directive. A severance regulation that began in Europe would impact producers well beyond the continent. Any large company selling a designated substitute in Europe, whether based in Paris, California or Shenzhen, might be required to register a product and begin paying a declining levy on its European sales once measurable displacement began.

A scheme like this would require innovative producers to think proactively about the severances their goods might provoke. If provenance labels and QR codes look backwards, following salmon to a pen or eggs to a farm, a public severance assessment would look forward, asking what function a new product performs, which commodities it is likely to displace and what regions are most exposed to change. After being triggered — presumably after crossing a published threshold of European sales or producing a measurable fall in demand for the original commodity — the levy would decline over a fixed number of years and flow into transition trusts in producing regions.

As fermentation-derived cocoa fats and flavors move from the laboratory into chocolate and ice cream, trusts in Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire might use levy proceeds to finance crop diversification, forest restoration and more locally owned processing. Some farmers might reposition land-grown cacao as a “heritage” good to be sold at a premium. But boutique cacao is no answer for the millions of people who now depend on the bulk trade. A bolder severance agreement could pay part of the obligation as equity or a temporary share of sales, allowing the trust to profit from the substitute’s growth instead of merely absorbing the old industry’s decline.

Peru has already managed several fishing transitions. A trust financed by levies on algal omega-3 sales could help convert industrial sites into food-grade fish-processing facilities, clean bays polluted by fishmeal production and support the scallop and oyster farms already operating along the Áncash coast. Such trusts would invite capture. Industries dependent on the older commodities would lobby for a share of the money, and administrators would face pressure to cushion every producer’s loss. But their administrators would be wise to avoid the fantasy of a frictionless market transition, continuing to underwrite the purchase of commodities like fish oil simply to keep demand alive after market demand has disappeared. India’s poppy fields show what happens when transition assistance hardens into permanent demand.

In the aquaculture facilities nestled in Norway’s Hardangerfjord, pellets made with oil from algae or engineered canola may look no different from today’s buckshot as they arc into salmon pens. The difference will appear thousands of miles away in Chimbote’s docks and plants, where a share of the new oils’ sales could help workers build new livelihoods from the infrastructure of the old industry.

Chemists have been removing place from product since they first learned to make madder red from coal tar. Emerging technologies could bring that upheaval to more places in quicker succession, and politics must now give those places the means to build a future after their markets have gone.

stories.body:
Far from the grand ambitions declared in Yalta in 1945, Shenzhen felt like a meeting in search of an agenda

It is arguably true, given it was the first such meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the US, that Thursday’s gathering in Shenzhen deserved the description of “historic”.

But in terms of tangible outcomes, it is unlikely to warrant the “new page in the history of diplomacy” that Vladimir Putin claimed had been written, and will instead be consigned to a smallish footnote in any future volume of the 21st century.

It’s true that the meeting could yet be an icebreaker and the start of a permanent new dialogue. It’s also true that each leader can return home with something from the 90 minutes they spent together.

Despite falling asleep during the main Apec summit, Donald Trump had a chance to show his proximity to two authoritarian leaders he admires. With Ukraine having destroyed Russia’s bridge into Crimea , the US president greeted Putin as not just a friend but almost a wartime ally.

The Russian president, although occasionally pushed to one side by protocol during the early photo opportunities, will be able to show back home that it is Moscow, and not his adversary Europe, let alone Ukraine, that commands the respect and attention of Trump and Xi Jinping . As such, the summit was a free gift to Putin, and underlined that Trump was no longer the leader of the free world, as the former British foreign secretary Jeremy Hunt commented.

From Putin’s perspective, a meeting in Berlin of the coalition of the willing was a sideshow. Europe’s attempts to isolate Russia had failed and the Asia-Pacific region had become the centre of the global economy, Putin boasted. His relationship with Trump, he said, despite the difficulties, was founded on “similar civilisational values”.

For Xi, it was a prestigious chance to play host and implicitly demonstrate that the era of American hegemony is over. No longer the sole arbiter in world affairs, the US, the consumer economy, must share the stage with China , the manufacturing giant, and Russia, the energy bank.

The trio’s brief joint statement covered four pretty disparate topics: boosting energy supply, reforming the United Nations, limiting the powers of the international criminal court (ICC) and a tentative commitment to discuss nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation.

For grandeur at a time of various global crises, these ambitions hardly matched Yalta in 1945 or even the declaration after the Tehran summit in 1943, when the leaders of the UK, US and Russia sat on the veranda of the British embassy and pledged that their countries would work together after the war to build a “world family of democratic nations” free of tyranny and oppression. Winston Churchill declaimed in Tehran: “In our hands we have the future of mankind.” Joseph Stalin went further. “History has spoiled us,” he said. “She has given us very great power and very great opportunities.”

Shenzhen, by contrast, felt like a meeting in search of an agenda. The vacuum was filled with platitudinous commitments to “maintain strategic stability and international security”, a task that – looking around the world – none of those in attendance are currently pursuing with great effect.

Perhaps technology, multipolarity and their own divisions mean even they do not have “very great power”. Certainly there were no accompanying plans for how to reform the UN, let alone boost energy production or show respect for international law – a subject Trump’s current favoured successor, Marco Rubio, had just disparaged in a speech as a plaything of the global elite.

It was the summit’s chief instigator, Putin, who was the most eager of the three to set the meeting in a historic context, describing China, Russia and the US as the victors of the second world war, in a deliberate slight to Britain. A pledge to “preserve and strengthen the system of international law” seemingly referred to ensuring certain world leaders were freed from the prospect of the ICC serving them with arrest warrants.

By coincidence, the other world court, the international court of justice (ICJ), found a state – Myanmar – guilty of genocide for the first time on the same day. The Shenzen statement did not name the ICJ as a target, beyond an oblique reference to the ICC and “other similar institutions”. Doubtless that is only because ICJ rulings can be dismissed with near impunity.

Xi, nervous that China’s status as protector of the global south might be damaged by being involved in a global superpower carve-up, stuck to a familiar script: “History tells us that when major powers are at peace, the world is secure. When they clash, there is chaos.”

It may be that behind the scenes, or at other events, serious progress is being made on how China might act as a guarantor of a peace deal with Iran, or on who should lead the UN through its coming phase of reform, or even on how Putin might bring himself to seek peace in Ukraine in a way that protects Ukrainian sovereignty.

For the moment, though, it looks as if what little history was made in Shenzhen was made for exclusively the wrong reasons.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A handful of men control the US economy. They have leveraged themselves to be – or seem – indispensable

Jensen Huang has said he would return to Nvidia as its CEO if its board requests it.

“I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said . “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

Huang, who admitted being unfaithful to his wife, resigned from Nvidia last week. US intelligence agencies have identified one of his alleged lovers as a spy for China. If true, Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips may have found their way there.

Beyond the tabloid headlines lies a much bigger story – a US economy that’s become dependent on the initiatives and decisions of a few powerful men who are too big to fail.

We tend to think of government as being authoritarian, democratic or somewhere in between. For the last 22 months, we’ve witnessed what happens when the US government turns authoritarian.

An economy can also be described along the same continuum.

Throughout most of the last century, the US economy was fairly democratic. Decisions about what was produced and at what price reflected the judgments of tens of thousands of corporate executives, managers and small-business owners – all of whom were trying to respond to consumers and investors. Through labor unions, workers also had some say.

But the US economy has become far more authoritarian.

In recent decades, it’s become concentrated in the hands of a few giant corporations. Economies of scale have enabled those corporations to spread their fixed costs over many goods and services, and the US government has nearly abandoned antitrust (anti-monopoly) enforcement.

Labor unions have shrunk from representing over a third of private-sector workers in the 1950s to just 6% today.

More recently – over the last five years – something else has occurred, especially in big tech, that’s pushed the economy much further toward authoritarianism.

A handful of men – among them, Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg, Larry Ellison, Tim Cook and Jensen Huang – have not only become the richest people in the world, with significant political clout. They also control the direction and pace of technologies on which the US and the world depend.

These men are, in fact, the authoritarians of the new economy. They have unparalleled power over every aspect of the lives of Americans and millions of others around the world. And they have leveraged themselves to be, or seem, too big to fail.

The leverage works like this.

Nvidia’s value depends on Jensen Huang.

Hours after Huang’s resignation last Thursday, Nvidia stock dropped 10.3% in pre-market trading, erasing approximately $490bn of Nvidia’s value by the time the market opened.

Since the start of the leadership controversy at Nvidia on 8 November, the company has lost about $800bn in market value.

The AI industry, in turn, depends on Nvidia. Nvidia controls about 90% of the global market share of advanced AI chips. It has also become the major financier for the entire AI industry. Some call Nvidia the “ central bank of AI ”.

Nvidia’s $5tn market value (before 8 November) equaled about 8% of the total value of the S&P 500.

The US economy, in turn, depends on the AI industry. In the first quarter of 2025, the buildouts of datacenters using Nvidia chips accounted for 92% of US economic growth. Over the past two years, AI has been responsible for roughly half of America’s overall growth.

This huge leverage also works in reverse. Analysts fear that Nvidia’s collapse could cause the AI bubble to burst, triggering a failure that could threaten the entire US, if not also the world, economy.

Most Americans’ 401(k)s are invested in giant index funds tied to the Nasdaq and S&P 500. The Nasdaq and S&P 500, in turn, are based largely on 10 huge corporations . These 10 corporations are all connected to Nvidia. Together, they comprise about 37% of the value of the entire US stock market.

What all this means is Jensen Huang may be too big to fail.

More than 177,000 people have so far signed a “Stand with Jensen” open letter demanding that Nvidia’s board of directors “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”. Signers include Elon Musk; the Y Combinator president, Garry Tan; the Epic Games CEO, Tim Sweeney; and thousands of self-reported Nvidia employees.

Huang is discussing a possible return to the company, though the chair of the company’s board has said it’s not considering the move . One Huang ally talks of a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia ‌CEO’s return, ‌and garner support from ‌Trump. “Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person told the Financial Times, adding that the efforts have Huang’s support.

Trump told reporters on Monday that he “would not mind” if Huang were reinstated as Nvidia CEO, adding that he thought Huang had “learned a big lesson”.

Exactly what “big lesson” did Trump have in mind? That it’s not a good look for the CEO of the US’s most valuable corporation to have a romantic relationship out of wedlock?

Or that such a CEO shouldn’t break the law by supplying America’s most advanced AI chips to China through a Chinese spy?

On Tuesday, it was announced that Huang has agreed to appear on 1 December before the House foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party and the House intelligence committee in transcribed interviews.

Even in an authoritarian economy, no CEO is above the law. Or is he? We may soon find out.

Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com . His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

A trilateral gathering is good news for China and Russia, but bad for the US – and its traditional allies

“H istoric” is a neutral descriptor, not a favourable one. Things can be unprecedented for good reason. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Thursday will be the first time that the leaders of the US, China and Russia have gathered for talks as a trio. The trilateral on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is striking, but it is not an achievement.

The lack of a clear agenda is telling: the spectacle really is the substance. Mr Trump sees international affairs in terms of spheres of influence. This meeting reinforces the obvious conclusion for the rest of the world – that they don’t get to sit at the table, only to be on the plate. Mr Xi promotes the notion of a multipolar world. Others would be more sympathetic if all three governments were not determinedly undermining multilateralism.

Mr Xi looks like the power broker bringing Moscow and Washington together, and the gracious host, in a city which showcases China’s economic and technological progress and aspirations. The contrast between the glossy metropolis and a US currently beset by glaring tech failures hitting everything from flights to banking is especially flattering. For Mr Putin, who gloated about the “humiliation” of Europe in the run-up, this meeting is an even clearer win, making him look like a superpower peer rather than the leader of a pariah nation with a struggling economy.

Mr Trump has got a red carpet embrace, another “first” to promote – preferable to headlines dwelling on the Republicans’ midterms disaster – and the congenial company of strongmen. His nation has less to celebrate. Mr Trump seems to see meeting longstanding US allies as at best a chore. His bruising tariffs and nakedly transactional approach to security, as well as his love of autocrats, have pushed countries like the Philippines – which hosted the US president en route to China – into hedging their bets.

Mr Trump is not expected to raise Nvidia and suspected Chinese espionage – perhaps not least because his closeness to Jensen Huang, the company’s ousted CEO, makes the issue at least as discomfiting for him as it is for Beijing. The US president is unlikely to embarrass the two countries that are central to Iran’s ability to resist his disastrous and illegal war, or to press China over its facilitation of Russia’s war against Ukraine . Ukraine and Taiwan have reason to be anxious any time he speaks to Mr Putin and Mr Xi. But the US president is as likely to undermine them, whether deliberately or otherwise, in bilaterals or via a throwaway remark.

Comparisons to the 1945 Yalta summit of Joseph Stalin, Franklin D Roosevelt and Winston Churchill – which divided up Europe – grotesquely overstate the importance of a meeting scheduled to last less than an hour. Mr Xi does not do spontaneity, and is unlikely to be lured into sudden announcements. And despite the surface amity, the three still have strongly competing interests. China’s threat to rare earths brought a trade truce, but skirmishes continue. Mr Trump has said he wants to talk about denuclearisation . While China is arming itself at worrying speed, its arsenal is still dwarfed by those of the US and Russia.

Talking to rivals and adversaries is not inherently unwise. Under another US president, a closely focused and carefully prepared trilateral on, for instance, disarmament might even be fruitful. This is not that world. This will not be that meeting.

stories.body:
Global energy watchdog forecasts huge rise as US and China turn to fossil fuels to power AI growth agendas

The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.

The Paris-based agency found that the breakneck pace of the industry’s growth means that within four years AI datacentres will consume an extra 350 terrawatt-hours of electricity every year, or more than the annual electricity consumption of Great Britain.

Its influential annual report warned that the world’s energy future was less certain after the impact of the Middle East war, which it has described as the greatest energy market disruption in history.

“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said the IEA’s executive director Fatih Birol.

Instead, it will be reshaped by the policy decisions governments make after the crisis to meet the increasing demand for energy to power a growing global population, the rising need for air-conditioning and a booming AI economy, the IEA said.

Datacentre developers have emerged as the world’s biggest corporate buyers of renewable energy to help fuel their servers which have a connection to local power grids. Despite this, the report showed that the appetite for fossil fuels is expected to grow even faster, particularly in the US and China.

By the end of the decade, around half of the electricity needed to power China’s AI datacentres will come from coal power plants, according to the IEA. The rest will come from renewable energy, with smaller amounts from nuclear reactors and very little from gas plants.

In contrast, the US is expected to rely on gas to provide about 60% of the electricity for its datacentres by 2030. There were plans for about 180GW of new gas-fired power plants linked to US datacentres in August this year, the agency said. That is almost as much new gas capacity as the total now installed across the European Union.

As a result of the growth in fossil fuel generation for datacentres, emissions associated with this sector were on track to rise by 70% by 2030, the IEA said.

The appetite for gas power among US datacentre developers is more than 16 times higher than in Canada, where the IEA identified plans for 11GW of gas generation to power their servers. In the rest of the world, AI developers have put forward plans for new gas plants with a combined capacity of just 4GW, the agency said.

This is because renewable energy is expected to play a greater role in supplying datacentres outside the US and China. In the EU, the IEA expects datacentres to rely on renewables for about 70% of their electricity by 2030 – followed by nuclear power, gas generation, and a very small amount of coal power.

The agency based its forecasts for the notoriously opaque industry on data showing the annual global shipment of AI servers, which have climbed eighteen-fold since 2020. It also used space-based imagery to track the buildout of 93 large “AI factories” around the world.

Its analysis suggests that the world’s datacentre capacity has climbed tenfold in the last 24 months to 17GW. By the time the AI factories were completed, their combined capacity was likely to be about 50GW, the IEA said.

The world’s existing stock of datacentres, including those with AI-optimised servers, now stands at 120GW, with 80% of this capacity in China, the US and the EU. A further 120GW will be built by the end of the decade under the IEA scenario often considered its central base case, of which three-quarters will be AI datacentres.

stories.title: Anthropic shares end first day of trading at $97 as Wall Street closes sharply lower – as it happened
stories.summary: All ⁠three major US stock indexes ⁠ended the session ​sharply lower after record-breaking IPO by maker behind AI agent Claude Anthropic closes first day of public trading at $1.3tn valuation Protesters rally in New York and San Francisco Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn? Anthropic needs to grow into its $1.5tn valuation, argues Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB: Anthropic’s triumphant IPO and its trillion dollar plus valuation is more typical of a mature company that has a history of strong fundamentals. Anthropic could not be more different. It has generated strong revenue growth, but only in the short term, added to this, it is still unprofitable. Anthropic is another major tech company that requires investors to have a lot of faith about the future generation of revenues based on technology that will change the world. It seems like plenty are willing to give it that faith, and it is having a huge impact on the broader market today. Continue reading...
