Summary

Anthropic shares closed about 17% higher on their first day of trading on Thursday, despite investor fears of a possible AI bubble and public anxiety over the technology. The shares ended the session at around $97, up from a record-breaking IPO price of $83, after opening at $111.50 and briefly valuing the creator of the Claude chatbot at about $2tn – making the AI giant’s debut the biggest in history. The company’s valuation after the close stands at around $1.3tn, down from the high of $2tn recorded earlier.

However, a 2% slump at the close suggests that Anthropic’s stellar debut wasn’t enough to carry the wider market, which struggled for much of the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average sank 2.2%, while the S&P 500 fell 2% and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.3%, preliminary data showed. The S&P 500 fell for a sixth straight day - its longest losing streak since 19 April 2024 – amid concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom and after the drama surrounding Nvidia following the fall of its CEO Jensen Huang last week dragged the company’s shares down.

Shortly before ringing the Nasdaq opening bell, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei issued a warning about the dangers of AI but said they weren’t inevitable. “We’ve always been honest that this techology has very real risks … from misuse of the technology by individuals or nation states, to economic disruption, to losing control of AI systems,” he said. “Avoiding them depends on the choices made by the people making AI. There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety, versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety.”

The paper fortunes of Anthropic’s seven co-founders have now reached a total of more than $180bn. We have profiled them here .

Anthropic’s listing will serve as a bellwether for the multitrillion-dollar artificial intelligence boom as the first frontier lab to be publicly traded. Wall Street investors and the entire global tech industry – in particular, OpenAI, the parent company of ChatGPT – will be watching closely how it fares on the public market as time goes on.

Democratic US senator Adam Schiff has penned an op-ed in the Wall Street Journal warning about “the systemic risk to the economy” posed by the AI industry – and demanding that Congress rule out a taxpayer-funded bailout should the sector collapse.

Highlighting the turmoil surrounding Nvidia since the spectacular exit of its CEO Jensen Huang, Schiff writes:

double quotation mark This technology [artificial intelligence] has boundless potential to enhance our lives and expand our individual and collective capacity. But as the turmoil around Nvidia reminds us, this swift and massive investment also carries significant risk that an industry downturn or a bubble could destabilize the American economy. In the first six days of the scandal involving Nvidia and its former CEO, the sector lost $500bn in value. Given the risks to our economy and investors, Congress must make sure that industry understands this: No company is too big to fail, and in the event of a financial collapse of the tech sector, there will be no taxpayer-funded bailout. The AI industry, after less than five years of market power, is already estimated to represent 3.6% of our nation’s economy. But much of its explosive build-out is financed by an opaque debt structure and expectations of increasing profitability. This may be the biggest economic gamble in American history , and policymakers should make clear that Congress and American taxpayers won’t act as its fail-safe should this industry falter under its own immense weight .

Schiff goes on to remind the reader: “We have seen this movie before.” Invoking the bank bailout of 2008, he writes: “ If these enormous bets fail, Big Tech and Wall Street billionaires will no doubt turn to Washington for emergency rescue, a path unfortunately well-trodden by corporate giants before them. But the risk should be borne by these companies and their investors, not working families.”

double quotation mark The billionaire investors may be taking this gamble with the assumption that as in 2008, they will be bailed out for failed investments and corporate risk-taking. Congressional majorities should be clear: We won’t bail them out.

Anthropic has made a blockbuster stock market debut – shattering already high expectations.

The AP has put together some numbers to help you understand Thursday’s IPO:

The amount in proceeds raised by the offering: $81bn. That makes Anthropic’s debut the biggest ever. Ahead of Thursday’s trading, it offered 980m shares priced at $83 each, putting Anthropic ahead of Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which set a previous record with its IPO proceeds of about $75bn in June.

Anthropic’s initial valuation: $1.5tn. The initial price per share was set at $83. But that spiked more than 30% to open at $111.50 a share — pushing the company’s total valuation by half a trillion dollars to $2.01tn just before noon ET.

By market close Thursday, Anthropic finished its first trading day at $97.17 per share. That’s still over 17% higher than its initial public offering price, and amounts to a market value of roughly $1.75tn. In June, SpaceX ended its first day of trading on the public market with a valuation of $2.1tn. Its market cap has since fallen to closer to $1.95tn.

Number of public companies that have reached the trillion-dollar club in the S+P 500: 11

Apple currently leads the pack at $5.1tn, followed by Microsoft ($3.8tn) and Nvidia ($3.6tn), among others. That does not count SpaceX and Anthropic, which also have joined the trillion-dollar club even though they aren’t in the S+P 500 index yet. Only in recent memory have major corporations been valued over $1tn. iPhone maker Apple was the first to pass that threshold, back in 2018 .

There are more than 8.2 billion people living on Earth today, per the US Census Bureau. If $1tn was divided among the entire population, each person would receive almost $122.

Anthropic ’s shares closed 17% higher on their first day of trading, at just over $97.

Wall Street closes sharply lower as Anthropic's debut fails to revive AI enthusiasm

It’s just gone 4pm ET, which means trading in New York has closed for the day. US stocks slumped at the close, after Anthropic ’s super-sized IPO failed to revitalize faded enthusiasm over artificial intelligence, as an early soar in its share price ebbed.

All ⁠three major US stock indexes ⁠ended the session ​sharply lower, with the benchmark S+P 500 logging its fifth straight session of losses.

According to preliminary data, the S+P 500 lost 148.39 points, or 2.03%, to end at 7,175.24 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 544.00 points, or 2.23%, to 23,885.88. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1,102.71 points, or 2.20%, to 49,095.46.

Anthropic’s record-setting IPO was priced late on Wednesday at $83 per share, and the stock opened at $111.50 shortly before noon. After the company’s market valuation ⁠briefly surpassed $2tn, its momentum began to lose steam.

Most chipmakers were lower, ‌including Micron and Broadcom, among others. And Nvidia marked its sixth straight session of losses after the chipmaker’s upbeat revenue forecast did little to lift sentiment.

The Wall Street investment bankers that worked on Anthropic’s blockbuster initial public offering are set to be awarded a record $550m in underwriting fees, according to the official filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.

That is more than they made on SpaceX , which set the previous record at $500m.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley will earn the biggest cut, taking over $200m between them.

Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?

Dan Milmo and Aisha Down

The paper fortunes of Anthropic’s seven co-founders reached a total of more than $180bn on Thursday as shares in their company started trading at a price ahead of expectations.

The opening price of $111.50 per share valued the entrepreneurs’ stakes – including chief executive Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela – at between $26.5bn and $27bn each. The founders have pledged to donate 80% of their shareholdings in Anthropic to philanthropic causes, which would equate to around $150bn at the current share price.

Other investors generating considerable wealth from the float and the late share price surge include the Hollywood actor Ashton Kutcher and Madonna’s manager, Guy Oseary , whose venture capital firm, Sound Ventures, reportedly owns 0.5% as an early investor. That stake would be worth $10bn at the opening price.

Anthropic has also committed 5% of its shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, which will “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”. The company has said some of the proceeds could be used to address AI’s impact on the job market , though fears the technology will lead to significant job losses have yet to be realised.

Anthropic’s IPO is widely expected to channel vast sums into the coffers of a powerful social movement called effective altruism, via the many millions of dollars that its 5,300 staff will have made from the flotation. EA, as it is known, crystallised on university campuses in the US and UK in the early 2010s. It encourages its members to donate a substantial portion of their income to a set of specific causes which it deems high-priority. These include things like pandemic prevention, biorisk, nuclear safety and – overwhelmingly – the risks posed by advanced AI.

Anthropic’s co-founders, including Dario Amodei, are associated with EA. Amodei took a pledge to donate his income through the organisation Giving What We Can, which is associated with the movement. However, he now disavows his association and has said he does not consider himself an effective altruist.

In 2023, he told The New York Times’ Hard Fork podcast he was “sympathetic to a number of the ideas” promoted by EA, but against “dividing people up into tribes”.

My colleagues have profiles of all co-founders here:

Here’s the clip of Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei , issuing a warning about the dangers of artificial intelligence, saying it has “very real” but “avoidable” risks, shortly before the company rang the opening bell at Nasdaq.

Richard Partington and Kalyeena Makortoff

Booming demand for artificial intelligence will force the world’s most powerful central banks to raise interest rates, the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned.

Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the Washington-based fund, said demand for AI hardware and related technology products was pushing up consumer prices around the world.

She said that, alongside the energy shock from the war in the Middle East , this was adding to inflationary pressures around the globe.

“ This calls for a tightening of monetary policy in many economies ,” she said.

Speaking at the 2026 Apec summit in Shenzhen , Georgieva warned that both factors would push global inflation to 4.7% this year. She added that the rapid rollout of AI was also contributing to stronger than expected economic growth in several countries, despite the headwinds from the Iran war.

Georgieva said that while the energy shock would eventually dissipate, “AI is for ever” – making it a significant driver of world trade, competitiveness, productivity and economic growth.

AI hardware and related tech products now account for more than one-tenth of the world goods trade, a share that is rapidly rising, she said. But some countries were benefiting more from investment than others.

“ To put it simply: you snooze, you lose ,” she added. “ Countries need digital infrastructure, labour markets and workers that are ready for AI, and risk mitigation – especially to control financial stability and cybersecurity risks. ”

Read the full report here:

Lisa Bonos in San Francisco

Sameer Shariff, co-founder and CEO of English language education company Cambly, noticed a buzz of energy among Anthropic employees as they were leaving the company’s headquarters in San Francisco yesterday.

Over the past two years, a few employees have left his company to join Anthropic. He’s been thinking about them today.

“I’m happy for them. It’s a big day for the market and for AI,” Shariff said, while chatting with a friend at Joe and the Juice in downtown San Francisco on Thursday. So far, “Anthropic has been funded by all these investors with the inside scoop. But this is a test of how Wall Street responds … all of a sudden the general public has access to participate.”

Shariff said he’s curious how the next six to 12 months will go. “I’m a big fan,” he added.

As we await the close of market valuation of Anthropic at the end of its first day on the market, Rebecca Walser, chief investment officer at US-based Walser Wealth Management, wrote: “Anthropic’s IPO is exactly what the markets need to revive overall sentiment, which has been depressed with all of the negativity in the AI complex over the past several weeks.”

Walser added: “It’s possible that Anthropic could see volatility and downside moves during the Jensen Huang Senate testimony after Thanksgiving, because that is likely to reignite AI fears.

“But if that happens, it could be a good entry point for investors who want to buy Anthropic.”

Lisa Bonos in San Francisco

On a drizzly morning in downtown San Francisco after a massive storm the day before, the mood was sleepy in the Andytown coffee shop atop Salesforce Tower Park. When asked about Anthropic’s IPO today, one barista said “What’s that?” — a clue that not everyone in this tech hub is obsessed with AI.

Anthropic workers do frequent the coffee shop, but they hadn’t seen any today, her colleague said. One patron, smiled when asked if he worked at the maker of Claude. “No, but I wish I did,” he said. Out on the street, foot traffic seemed lighter than normal, likely due to the weather. But still some tech workers trickled into their offices at 9:30 a.m.

“I wish I was in that building,” a Meta worker, who declined to give his name, said entering his downtown San Francisco office and gesturing to one of Anthropic’s offices across the street. His friends who work at Anthropic have “big plans for what to do with their newfound wads of cash,” he said. “Some people are planning to backpack Asia,” he said. But mostly, they plan to keep working and liquidate slowly, he added.

stories.title: PM urges social media companies to 'show some decency' and take down Brand video
stories.summary: The comments came after YouTube owner Google refused a government request to remove a clip posted by the wife of the jailed comedian in which he claims he is innocent.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 18 November 2026

Social media companies should "show some decency and take these videos down", the prime minister has said, following a government attempt to have a YouTube video featuring a message from the jailed comedian removed.

The site's owner Google refused a government request to remove the clip posted by Brand's wife in which he claims his innocence, Whitehall sources have told the BBC.

Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Speaking following a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin, Andy Burnham said it was "time that we focus on the victims and think about them," rather than "hearing from a convicted criminal".

He said: "I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down. Why are we having to hear from him. We shouldn't be and certainly [victims] shouldn't be hearing from him."

But when pressed by the reporter if he wanted to change the law to take action, he replied: "I wouldn't leap to that. I would first say to the social media companies show some responsibility here, think of the victims - that's the main thing.

"Show some decency and take these videos down."

Google told BBC News it was "aware of the new content and our teams are investigating".

It added: "We suspended Russell Brand's channel from the YouTube Partner Program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then."

On Sunday, Laura Brand shared a video on their Sunday Service channel on the website and read out a message from her husband in which he said: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."

The Prison Service of England and Wales asked for the video to be removed, on the basis it was offensive to Brand's victims and had reached a substantial audience.

A Ministry of Justice (MoJ) spokesperson said while "removal ultimately depends on the platform's own terms", the department strongly believes "YouTube should remove this content".

Russell Brand prison message 'appalling' and being investigated, No 10 says Published 3 days ago

Minister criticises media for 'amplifying' Russell Brand's prison message Published 1 day ago

Met Police investigating more 'potential criminal allegations' about Brand Published 10 November

The BBC was initially told a minister had met Google to request the deactivation of Brand's account.

The MoJ later clarified the request had focused on the controversial video, and it is now understood a minister did not meet Google and the request was made via an established mechanism the prison service has with tech companies to request deletion of material.

The BBC has been told that Google declined the request, saying that its rules had not been broken, but housing minister Matthew Pennycook - who described the video as "abhorrent" - told BBC Breakfast that the government remained in "close dialogue" with the company.

Jess Phillips, the former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the government "doesn't have the power to enforce that this video is taken down".

"It relies on YouTube, in this instance... to do the right thing, which is a much, much broader argument about whether Ofcom codes that are in the Online Safety Act are there actually to protect women," she said.

An Ofcom spokesperson said in a statement that the current guidance was ultimately voluntary, and "any changes to the legislation to make it mandatory would be a matter for government and parliament".

Phillips, describing Brand as an "absolute narcissist", suggested it was "very likely" the government would look at introducing a second online safety act to address gaps in the current regulatory framework.

"Before, we haven't had prisoners who had massive YouTube followings," she said. "This is an entirely new era."

However, the BBC understands there are no new plans to update or bring fresh legislation governing online platforms as a result of Brand's case.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she would not immediately demand Google remove the video, if she was in power - although agreed it was concerning "if people in prison are able to use other conduits to send messages".

Badenoch told Today, YouTube was a private platform, and demanding content be taken down "without looking at exactly whether a law has been broken is not where I would start from".

"If we want to make legislation for that, then we can look at that. But I'm quite worried about government intervening," she added.

Connie Shaw of the Free Speech Union backed Badenoch's comments, saying that "if we want to protect everyone's free speech, we have to protect the free speech of even the most heinous people".

Speaking to the BBC's Politics Live, she said that it would "set a very dangerous precedent if we said that Russell Brand's wife is not able to express the fact that he rejects the fact that he has been found guilty".

Brand's message has prompted an investigation into whether he had broken prison rules.

Downing Street previously called the message "clearly appalling", adding: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the case was being "urgently investigated, and I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules".

Prisoners' phone conversations are routinely recorded, but not necessarily listened to by prison authorities. If Brand is found to have breached the rules, possible repercussions could include a temporary phone ban or live monitoring of his calls.

In 2022 notorious inmate Charles Bronson reportedly had restrictions placed on his phone use after he sent Sky News an unauthorised audio message about his bid for parole.

In recent years, Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer and has a large following.

Mia Latter, a woman who has made allegations against Brand, said she found the message shared by Laura Brand "upsetting" and was appalled to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".

Latter, 37, has alleged she was raped by the comedian when she was 16. She was not a complainant in his recent criminal trial and he denies her claims.

"I just felt for those women that stood trial and everything they went through," she told BBC.

The video and the Brands' YouTube account are still available on the site, and also still active is Brand's X account, where a message last appeared on 11 November.

"There was never a Russell Brand, according to @meta," it read, referring to Meta's decision to disable Brand's social media accounts on Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp.

"Thank God for @elonmusk," the message added, referring to X's owner, before concluding: "Stay tuned."

The BBC has approached X for comment; Musk himself has criticised Brand's conviction for historical sex offences.

Children's minister Josh MacAlister told the Today programme the Meta decision provided a clear template for taking action.

"Meta's community standards prohibit accounts owned by or run on behalf of convicted sex offenders, and it's as simple as that," he said. "Google should take this down."

stories.title: UK to provide Ukraine with 1,000 long-range strike drones
stories.summary: The prime minister made the announcement at a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at Downing Street last month

Published 19 November 2026, 09:10 GMT

The UK will provide Ukraine with 1,000 long-range strike drones to target Russia beyond the front line, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced.

The drone support was announced at a meeting in Berlin of Ukraine's allies, the Coalition of the Willing, and is part of a new £260m package to boost its war defences this winter.

The government said the drones are able to fly up to 625 miles (1,000km) and carry heavier warheads, enabling Ukraine to target military production facilities.

The move is the latest sign of a growing British involvement in drone technology for Ukraine. The government said 80% of the package will be spent in the UK.

The Berlin talks came as US President Donald Trump is meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese Premier Xi Jinping.

Ahead of that meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in China, Trump said both he and Xi want to see an end to the Ukraine war.

EU-UK talks going down to the wire, says No 10 Published 37 minutes ago

Trump says summit with Xi and Putin in China is 'making history'

Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war Published 1 day ago

Crimean Bridge attacked again, Russia says Published 9 hours ago

In a statement released ahead of the latest meeting of the group of 36 countries committed to supporting Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire or peace agreement - the government said the UK is also building maritime, logistical and surveillance drones to help Ukraine's war effort.

Burnham, who co-chaired the meeting, had said the UK must do everything it can to make sure Ukraine can defend itself from Russian attacks throughout the winter.

Speaking at a press conference after the talks, Burnham said the mood of the coalition is "more determined than ever to stay the course" in support of Ukraine.

He welcomed the presence of US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff at the meeting and described Russia as "perhaps the biggest losers" of the conflict, as he referred to casualties they have suffered.

Burnham said: "This clearly has got to be a moment to move towards peace because of the US involvement that we've seen today and the progress clearly that is being made.

"Europe is ready to enter these negotiations, we are clear about what we will accept and what we won't accept, but we are also clear that we stand with Ukraine today, tomorrow, for as long as it takes, until this unjust war is over."

Before this latest support package was announced, government figures put the amount of support provided by the UK for Ukraine since Russia invaded the country in February 2022 at £35.5bn. , external

In recent days, Ukraine has struck oil refineries in southern Russia, and has repeatedly hit the Crimean Bridge - a significant logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.

Meanwhile, Russian forces have been focused on knocking out power in Ukraine before winter with attacks on critical infrastructure.

The UK is among a number of countries also supplying Ukraine with lightweight missiles which are being used to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.

Ukraine's strike rate is now close to 70%, more than double what it was just a couple of months ago, Downing Street said.

The UK also pledged further air defence support this week and sanctioned Russia's 10 major oil producers.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the government was delivering on a promise for more support for Ukraine at the Budget.

"Ukraine's frontline is the frontline for freedom and democracy, and we will stand with them for as long as it takes," he said.

Meanwhile, on Friday Burnham will head to Brussels for a UK-EU summit, where both sides hope to unveil new agreements on food, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime.

stories.title: Timetable set out for dismantling leasehold system in England and Wales
stories.summary: Under the government's plans, a ban on the sale of most new leasehold flats is expected around 2031.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 19 November 2026, 02:02 GMT

The government has set out a timetable for when the leasehold system in England and Wales will be dismantled.

Under the plans, most new flats - with only limited exemptions - will be sold as commonhold, where residents collectively own and manage their buildings.

The government says a modernised commonhold model is expected to be up and running around 2029, followed by a ban on the sale of most new leasehold flats, expected around 2031.

Meanwhile, a £250 cap on ground rents - the annual fee paid by leaseholders to their freeholder - is expected to come into force in 2028, six months after a new law passes.

Ground rents will then be reduced to a "peppercorn" rate - which is effectively nothing - after 40 years.

There are around five million leasehold homes in England and Wales, where people own the right to occupy a property via a lease for a limited number of years from a freeholder.

Under commonhold, there is no ground rent or expiring lease.

On Thursday, the government introduced the Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill , external to Parliament.

In order to become law, the bill would first need to be approved by both Houses of Parliament, a process that will take several months, and the measures in the bill will not come into force straight away.

The government says the bill will also make it easier for existing leaseholders to convert to commonhold.

Under the plans, instead of all leaseholders having to agree before a building can convert, only 50% will have to support the move.

Labour MP Abena Oppong-Asare, who chairs the Commons Housing Committee, welcomed the bill but said "leaseholders have been waiting far too long for successive governments to tackle the unfair leasehold system".

She added: "I hope the government will consider accelerating the timetable for introducing the £250 cap on ground rent so that leaseholders can see those savings sooner rather than later."

In an interview with the BBC, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner was challenged over whether the government was moving too slowly on leasehold reform.

In response, she said leasehold was an area "fraught with legal challenge".

She added: "We've got the balance right we believe, making sure that we've done the pre-legislative work, to ensure that we've consulted as much as we need to, so that we can implement these changes."

'Continuous torture cell'

Fozia Malik lives in a one-bedroom flat in Oldham and says her ground rent will go up from £150 to £300 in January. That is alongside service charges of more than £4,000 a year.

Malik says her block of flats has been plagued by a number of problems, including fire safety issues and rising costs.

The managing agent for her building says the service charges are due to costs that are out of its control and high insurance because of fire safety issues.

But Malik says she would "never" buy a leasehold flat again, describing it as a "continuous torture cell".

Fozia Malik says she would "never" buy a leasehold flat again

When she bought her flat, Malik assumed the system would work in the same way it does in Pakistan, where she grew up, and in most other countries, where buying a home also means owning a share of the land it sits on.

However, in England, most flats are sold on a leasehold basis. That gives the buyer the right to occupy and use a property for a set period of time, but the freeholder retains ultimate ownership of the building and the land.

Systems based on shared ownership and collective management - such as commonhold - are already standard in many parts of the world, including Australia, New Zealand, the US, Canada and much of continental Europe. They give residents ownership of their home and a stake in the building's common areas.

Scotland does not have leasehold tenures, while Northern Ireland has just a handful of leasehold properties.

The government says its reforms are intended to bring England and Wales more closely in line with other other countries around the world, which do not have leaseholds.

Risk of two-tier system

Campaigners have welcomed many of the reforms, but questioned what happens to the millions of people who already own leasehold homes.

Giles Grover, from the campaign group End Our Cladding Scandal, says there is a risk the proposed changes will create a two-tier system of those buying new homes and existing leaseholders.

He began campaigning on behalf of flat owners following the Grenfell Tower tragedy.

He said: "It's so complicated, will the measures that are being introduced actually benefit everyone?"

The National Leasehold Campaign welcomed the "landmark legislation", but said: "The true test of these reforms will be whether the millions of existing leaseholders already living under the leasehold system are given an affordable and accessible route to commonhold."

Giles Grover, from the campaign group End Our Cladding Scandal, says there is a risk the proposed changes will create a two-tier system

The Residential Freehold Association, which represents the UK's largest freeholders, says the bill is "an unprecedented abuse of property rights".

It says the legislation could wipe billions from the value of pension funds, which have invested heavily in ground rents.

Many leaseholders have also complained of high service charges, which they have no control over and must pay for the management and maintenance of their building.

The government says new measures added to the legislation will require building owners to check their condition, plan for works and build up funds ahead of time, helping to reduce the risk of homeowners suddenly facing huge bills for repairs.

Other measures in the legislation include:

Abolishing forfeiture, where leaseholders can be threatened with losing their home over unpaid charges as low as £350

Giving ministers the power to cap excessive permission and administration fees, for things like asking to keep a pet or replace a front door

Making it cheaper and easier to extend a lease or buy the freehold.

Ibrar Ali was attended by emergency services on Manse Street in Bradford

Published 19 November 2026, 15:43 GMT

A councillor has been seriously injured after being stabbed while undertaking his duties in Bradford.

Bradford Moor councillor Ibrar Ali was attacked at about 11:04 GMT on Manse Street, according to the deputy leader of Your Bradford Independent Group, councillor Ishtiaq Ahmed.

West Yorkshire Police said a 32-year-old man had been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder and was being held in custody.

The force added there was "no information to suggest that this is a politically motivated incident at this time".

Ali is believed to have been injured on Thornbury Avenue, before being driven to the nearby Manse Street where emergency services attended, according to police.

A force spokesperson previously said the suspect had climbed on to the roof of a property on Thornbury Avenue following the incident and was later brought down.

Councillor Ibrar Ali was stabbed while walking around Bradford Moor

Ahmed said Ali was undergoing emergency surgery at Leeds General Infirmary after being stabbed in the leg. He said Ali was in a stable condition but had lost a lot of blood.

"My thoughts are with him and his family and loved ones. It's an extremely distressing time," said Ahmed.

"We shouldn't have to fear for our personal safety because we have chosen to serve the public.

"There should be no normalisation of violence in our democratic life."

Responding to the incident in his Bradford East constituency, Labour MP Imran Hussain described the incident as "horrific" and "deeply disturbing".

"My thoughts and prayers are with councillor Ibrar Ali and his family," said Hussain.

"No elected politician should feel under threat or fear for their safety while carrying out their duties and serving their community."

Councillor Ibrar Ali was attacked on Manse Street

Ch Supt Richard Padwell urged anyone with information to contact police.

"This is a serious incident where a local councillor has been stabbed in the street and our thoughts are with him, his family and colleagues at this difficult time," he said.

"Whilst the investigation is in the early stages, there is nothing to suggest that this incident is politically motivated at this time."

Ali is a community development manager at charity The Leap.

He has worked with community organisations Bradford Moor Pass and was one of the founders of Leeds Road Festival.

He was first elected as a councillor in the May local election, replacing the previous Labour representatives.

stories.body:
Sanae Takaichi cuts lonely figure at airport, a move by China that is being linked to the simmering row over Taiwan

Apec’s Chinese hosts went out of their way to give world leaders a warm welcome as they arrived in Shenzhen this week. Military bands played, dozens of cheering young men and women waved colourful bouquets, and senior officials offered hugs and handshakes on the tarmac.

But there was one exception: Japan ’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi .

The red carpet was rolled out for her arrival at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport, but Takaichi, on her first visit to China since taking office just over a year ago, had to make do with a modest guard of honour and a welcome from a relatively junior Chinese government official.

The contrast in hospitality was impossible to ignore. Donald Trump was personally greeted by Chinese leader Xi Jinping as he stepped off Air Force One, while Vladimir Putin was met by Cai Qi, a senior Communist party official and one of Xi’s closest aides.

The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese , beamed as he walked past rows of women in white shirts and pink skirts while soldiers from the People’s Liberation Army stood to attention, bayonets fixed. South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, and the country’s first lady, Kim Hea Kyung, were given similar VIP treatment.

Takaichi, on the other hand, was met off her plane by Zhang Qiyue, China’s former ambassador to Greece, a position below those who greeted other leaders. Zhang, though, does have a connection with Japan: her father, Zhang Shu, was once China’s ambassador in Tokyo.

Many are linking China’s frosty welcome to a simmering row over Taiwan that began shortly after Takaichi made her diplomatic debut at the 2025 Apec summit in South Korea, where she and Xi vowed to build “constructive and stable” relations.

Less than a fortnight later, Takaichi triggered a diplomatic crisis when she told MPs that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could trigger the deployment of her country’s self-defence forces if the conflict posed an existential threat to Japan, whose westernmost island, Yonaguni , is just 100km from Taiwan.

Insisting that Japan could exercise its right to collective self-defence – or coming to the aid of an ally, namely the US – Takaichi said Tokyo had to plan for a crisis in the Taiwan strait.

Beijing has not ruled out the use of force to annex Taiwan – a self-governing democracy it regards as a Chinese province – under what it calls “reunification”.

China’s foreign ministry condemned her remarks at the time as “wrongful and dangerous,” while online, many accused Japan’s leader of dragging her country back into prewar militarism.

The dispute soured economic and cultural ties. Beijing warned Chinese citizens not to take holidays or study in Japan , claiming, without evidence, that they would face threats to their safety. Grassroots exchanges were called off and the Chinese releases of Japanese films postponed indefinitely.

Panda diplomacy also took a hit in January, when Xiao Xiao and Lei Lei, a pair of giant pandas that had been kept at Ueno Zoo in Tokyo, departed Japan, leaving the country without one of the animals for the first time since 1972, when Tokyo and Beijing normalised diplomatic ties.

As Xi, Trump and Putin prepared to hold historic three-way talks in Shenzhen on Thursday, Takaichi managed only a cordial handshake and a few words with Xi – another reminder that Japan-China relations have yet to come in from the cold.

stories.summary: The former home and foreign secretary has been a London Assembly member and fire authority chair.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Sir James was named as the Conservative Party candidate on Thursday

Published 19 November 2026, 10:33 GMT

Former home secretary and foreign secretary Sir James Cleverly has been selected as the Conservative candidate for mayor of London.

The MP for Braintree in Essex was chosen in a poll of party members in London, winning 86% of the vote.

Sir James saw off a challenge from Westminster City councillor Festus Akinbusoye and Richmond Park parliamentary candidate Sara Gezdari.

He said London's "best days are ahead if we make a change at the forthcoming election". The next mayoral election will be in May 2028.

'It's shameful'

Labour incumbent Lord Khan, first elected in 2016, is yet to confirm whether he will seek a fourth term.

Sir James, a former head of the London Fire Authority, was widely expected to win the nomination after he stood down from the shadow cabinet in August.

He said he would not seek re-selection as the candidate in his Essex seat at the next general election.

At the announcement of the result, he said Lord Khan was "letting London down".

Sir James added: "People are leaving London, or not choosing to come here in the first place - businesses, job creators, families leaving London - and by the time of the election in 2028, Khan will have been mayor for 12 years, and those two things are related.

"The problems London faces are the symptoms. Khan is the cause. When I ask Londoners, 'Do you feel safe walking home at night?', the answer is no."

"It's shameful, it's a failure, and it's not just crime.

"We have had the worst period of housebuilding since the Second World War and only the highest-earning Londoners can afford the cheapest houses in London."

'Crime went up'

Bridget Phillipson, chair of the Labour Party, said: "James Cleverly has a record of failure and now wants to inflict his disastrous CV on London.

"He backed a no-deal Brexit and Liz Truss's disastrous mini-budget, voted for cuts to policing and youth services and opposed action to clean up London's air.

"Londoners should never forgive and never forget the damage the Conservatives did to our capital."

Sir James, an Army reservist, represented the Tories on the London Assembly before his election as MP for Braintree in 2015.

After rising through the backbenches, he unsuccessfully ran for Conservative Party leader in 2024, losing out to Kemi Badenoch.

The only other confirmed party choice for the mayoral race is Laila Cunningham from Reform UK, whose candidacy was announced in January.

She told BBC London: "It's the Conservatives that cut police, they cut the magistrates' numbers, crime went up, they politicised stop and search, and as a result knife crime has gone up massively."

'Take London backwards'

Sarah Olney and Rob Blackie are both candidates for the Liberal Democrats' nomination.

Olney, the MP for Richmond Park, told BBC London the city "really needs a champion but the Tories are not going to be able to effectively hold Labour to account given their record in the capital".

She added: "James Cleverley simply is not a credible contender for mayor of London.

"In the past decade he has enthusiastically championed Brexit and he was a huge supporter of Liz Truss's mini budget and both of those things have done so much damage to London."

Should Lord Khan decide not to run again, there are a number of London Labour figures with ambitions to be the next mayor, including MPs Dawn Butler and Rosena Allin-Khan.

The Green Party, which won outright control of three London boroughs at the local elections in May, leads minority administrations in Haringey and Lambeth, and runs Southwark in coalition with the Lib Dems, has yet to begin the process of picking a candidate for the 2028 mayoral race.

Mayor of Hackney Zoë Garbett, who was the Green candidate in the 2024 mayoral election, said Sir James would "take London backwards".

She added: "Cleverly's platform is all about dividing our communities and making people's lives harder and more expensive."

stories.title: Badenoch defends amputee marathon runners claim in benefits cut row
stories.summary: Paralympian Richard Whitehead had accused the Conservative leader of "weaponising" his sporting success.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 19 November 2026, 12:51 GMT

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has defended her suggestion that because double amputees run marathons more disabled people should work instead of claiming benefits.

Badenoch had used the example when setting out her party's plans to cut welfare spending by £36bn a year .

Her comments were criticised by Paralympian Richard Whitehead, who accused her of "weaponising" his sporting success, while Prime Minister Andy Burnham called the Tory leader's words "crass and insensitive".

But in an interview with the BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Badenoch stood by the remarks, insisting that "if people even with significant problems can work, then those who have ADHD and mild anxiety should go to work".

Asked if she accepted the comments were insensitive, Badenoch said: "No, no, no. I do not accept it. I will speak the truth, and I will say what I believe is common sense. I will speak the truth, and I will say what I believe is common sense.

"What I know is that if people can work, then we should encourage them to work."

Badenoch acknowledged she had used "extreme examples to illustrate things", but added: "If someone can do that, then yes, your condition of ADHD or anxiety is mild."

"I will say things as they are. People may disagree with things that I say, and that's fine, this is a free country, people are free to disagree, but they know where I'm coming from," she said.

"I start from first principles: If you can work, you should work, and the Conservative Party is going to help you get a job."

Government backs welfare shake-up to prevent 'lost generation' Published 2 days ago

What are the government's options for reducing welfare spending? Published 29 October

In a speech setting out the Conservative Party's welfare plans last week, Badenoch said: "The reality is that millions of people can and do contribute to our economy, to their families, to their communities even when they face serious challenges.

"Double amputees run marathons. People who are housebound do wonderful creative work from home. People with autism run some of the biggest tech companies in the world."

Responding to her speech, Whitehead - a double amputee marathon runner who has won four Paralympic medals - said he was "gobsmacked that somebody's sporting success would be weaponised in this way" , external .

In a post on social media , external , he also said: "Disability should never be judged through isolated examples of individual achievement, but through an understanding of the barriers people and families face every day.

"The fact that some double-leg amputees can run marathons does not mean that disability support is unnecessary.

"Equally, the fact that some people with ADHD thrive despite limited support does not mean that others do not need meaningful assistance."

Richard Whitehead celebrates after winning the mens 200m in 2016

As part of their plans to cut welfare spending, the Conservatives have proposed stopping people from claiming disability benefits for "milder mental health issues and neurodiversity conditions such as anxiety, depression and ADHD", as well as "routine back and joint pain".

The party says its proposals to overhaul sickness and disability benefits would save £13.7bn a year.

It would also invest £1bn into health support, so people no longer eligible for cash benefits can access treatment to support their conditions instead.

stories.title: The Brexit debate is back – and there are nerves about what happens next
stories.summary: Many of the names and arguments that defined the Brexit period are emerging again, as the debate over the UK being part of the EU is back on the agenda.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 19 November 2026, 11:48 GMT

"Stop Me If You Think You've Heard This One Before" sang Morrissey, as part of The Smiths in 1987, shortly before the band's acrimonious divorce.

It's a lyric Brexit veterans might be humming to themselves this week. Maybe even the prime minister, who is an avid fan of the Manchester band.

Some of the names - and arguments - that defined the Brexit period inside and outside Parliament are starting to emerge again, as the debate about the UK's relationship with the EU returns.

"It's like déjà vu with knobs on," said one veteran of the Leave campaign to us.

A new group called Stay Out has been set up, backed by figures who were part of the official Leave campaign in 2016. Boris Johnson has been back in the headlines, saying he still thinks Britons would choose to be outside the bloc.

Pro-EU groups such as the European Movement are raising their voices, pointing to the range of politicians, diplomats and academics they have supporting their argument. And a steady stream of Labour figures are now emerging to say they want to rejoin.

The former Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy made the argument on the BBC on Wednesday , saying Labour should go into the next election backing renegotiating membership of the EU and then putting that to people in another referendum.

He joins a list of cabinet ministers under Sir Keir Starmer who want to revisit EU membership; a list that includes former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, former Business Secretary Peter Kyle and former Welsh Secretary Jo Stevens. Others who served around Sir Keir's cabinet table think the same privately.

That is significant. Yes, they all backed Remain in 2016. But these are figures who were part of a government elected on a manifesto saying it was important to make Brexit work.

They set red lines in that manifesto because they thought the public had moved on. But they have now decided to say - most of them very publicly - that they think the picture has changed and the UK needs to think again.

The prime minister has opened the door to all options, from single market membership to rejoining the customs union to a referendum on full membership.

But in recent days, his language has softened a little from the clear commitment in his party conference speech that around the time of this Friday's summit he would "lay out to the country" the different options for Britain's long-term relationship with Brussels.

After some confusion about when this would take place, the government now says this will happen around the time that Burnham presents his 10-year plan, right before Parliament's Christmas break.

Burnham's allies say this will allow him to tie his EU policy more closely to his domestic agenda, arguing that a different arrangement with Europe would help with his other priorities such as the cost of living and re-industrialisation.

Others worry that the all-consuming nature of the EU debate means that it will drown out the other parts of the 10-year plan.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Watch: 'Hard Brexit we were given not good enough for Britain,' says Burnham

What remains unclear is the timeframe for the process that will follow Burnham setting out what he sees as the different Brexit options.

The prime minister has always been clear that Labour's commitments in its 2024 manifesto not to rejoin the single market or the customs union - let alone the EU altogether - still stand until the next general election.

And it was to those manifesto red lines that Burnham returned when asked about rejoining the EU at PMQs on Wednesday.

Yet those would not preclude Burnham initiating negotiations now on an arrangement breaking those red lines, which would take effect after the next general election.

Nevertheless, some on the prime minister's own side ponder that - having turned the volume up on the whole issue this autumn - he might be wise to turn it down a little in the new year, so it doesn't risk drowning out other things ministers want to talk about.

Andy Burnham is a prime minister who likes to explore things out loud. It's part of what he sees as a new way of doing politics, where he answers questions honestly and is prepared to discuss ideas while they are being formed, not just after they are a settled position.

It is a style that seeks to present a sense of a desired direction, even if some of the specifics end up being walked back from.

But even though it might be some time before the government has an official position on the future relationship, plenty of people are discussing what might happen next.

"It is all go again! My inbox is full of the same old stuff I thought I'd seen the back of years ago," one senior figure told us.

There are some nerves in the Labour Party about what might happen next. MPs who we have spoken to hold a range of views, which shows why this won't be plain-sailing.

Some are worried about re-opening the debate, calling it "toxic".

Others worry that the prime minister could disappoint pro-EU voters if he doesn't go far enough.

Others still wonder if the argument has changed enough that voters would decide differently in a new referendum.

"Both sides need fresh arguments, not the ones we all got tired of last time," said one.

"If this just looks like politicians wanting to rejoin because they never got over leaving then it's dead on arrival.

"If we can show that actually this is being led by businesses, by farmers, by different parts of society who need to rejoin because of the ways Brexit has harmed them, then it's a different matter," said another.

And what would the new EU the UK could rejoin look like?

Some Labour MPs ponder that the EU is changing – with the possibility of more right-wing leaders at the top table. They question whether they would want to be part of that.

EU-UK talks going down to the wire, says No 10 Published 37 minutes ago

Burnham to set out options next month for long-term EU relationship Published 1 day ago

The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left Published 1 day ago

UK lost more than it gained from Brexit, Burnham says ahead of EU summit Published 3 days ago

A long standing diplomat from an EU member state said that the possibility of political change within the EU, alongside the recent offer of associate membership to Canada and at least the possibility of a potential future arrangement with Ukraine after any peace deal, could mean Brussels becomes more open to looser forms of membership that it has not been willing to consider before.

But then there is Scotland. If the government backs another EU vote, some Scottish MPs worry it adds to the argument for another vote on Scottish independence.

Despite the warnings, plenty of MPs are delighted that the Europe debate is back on the agenda.

One summed it up like this: "It doesn't really matter to me at this point where the PM is heading on this – it's all good for appealing to progressive voters. Just being seen to talk about this even without it necessarily being clear what we're going to do is a big change from before."

That seems to be a prevailing mood at the moment. Lots of Labour MPs are happy the EU debate is back. But not all of them.

Andy Burnham will on Friday sign a new deal with the EU which ministers believe will drive economic growth and cut red tape for British businesses. It will be heralded as a new moment for the relationship.

But how much further could the reset go?

The government hasn't decided yet - but plenty of others have their own views.

stories.body:
In a world carved into continental blocs by authoritarians, Britain has to make common cause with its neighbours

In the chronicles of 21st-century diplomacy few statements have caused as much offence with as few words as Barack Obama’s 2014 description of Russia as a “regional power” .

Vladimir Putin’s politics were defined then, as now, by vengeful resentment of his country’s relegation from superpower status after the cold war. His worldview is warped by a paranoid conviction that Nato never stopped striving to deepen that humiliation, even after the USSR had unravelled. From his Kremlin throne, the Russian president expects to be treated as a colossus of world history. It is hard to overstate how bitterly he hated being dismissed by Obama as a geopolitical B-lister.

In Donald Trump , Putin has a ready supplier of balm to soothe his injured vanity. The US president has a shallow, venal concept of power. He is impressed by gilded palaces and heavily armed thugs. He feels thwarted by American democracy and envies tyrants who operate without equivalent restraint. Since Trump measures greatness in a country by its leader’s contempt for smaller nations and appetite for self-enriching plunder, he willingly promotes Russia back to the top tier.

That is the significance to Putin of a three-way summit with Trump and China’s Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Thursday. It confers trappings of parity with the world’s two genuine superpowers. That is a win for Russia, regardless of whether anything of substance is agreed.

The agenda is vague. The Chinese foreign ministry has said the discussion will focus on “ safeguarding world peace ” and “promoting strategic stability in major-power relations”. Xi will be satisfied with the projection of China as convener of a new world order. Trump has said he expects the conversation to cover denuclearisation, Iran, trade and “my favourite subject, Ukraine”.

The image of three leaders calibrating the balance of global power has been compared to Yalta, February 1945: Roosevelt, Stalin and Churchill drawing up plans for postwar Europe . That was a week-long conference where military allies were settling the fate of a defeated enemy. The analogy is revealing mostly as an expression of anxiety in those who will not be present.

For many Europeans, Yalta conjures memories of cynical partition, with eastern nations condemned to decades of Soviet captivity. The fear in Kyiv is that Putin will use his privileged access to Trump’s ear to pour in poisonous theories about the origins of the Ukraine war and how to end it – a twisted narrative of Nato provocation, irresistible Russian superiority and the need for Europe to stop wasting money and US military hardware on a losing cause.

The exclusion of European democracies from the room in Shenzhen is partly just a function of the conversation happening on the sidelines of a summit for countries with Pacific coasts. But it probes a deep strategic insecurity. Ukraine’s continental allies have asserted their rights to be part of any peace process but not found a way to turn that entitlement into a collective position, coordinated by a figure with diplomatic gravitas.

After a round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi last week, Jared Kushner, one of Trump’s envoys, made the reassuring statement that a deal could not be done “without Europeans being at the table”. By contrast, Russia’s chief negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, accused the Europeans of lacking serious intent to find solutions. He dismissed their delegation to the Gulf as “tourists” who might as well “chat in the hotel bar”.

That is standard Kremlin trolling, but it cuts with a shard of truth. It points to an old problem, often described with the apocryphal tale of Henry Kissinger complaining that there was no number to call when he wanted to speak to Europe. The challenge is more acute today. The institutional and economic foundations of European influence are under assault. Trump is ambivalent at best about Nato. His administration is protectionist and nationalist. Maga ideology casts liberal democratic Europe as a moribund civilisation erasing itself with mass immigration.

China treats Europe as a bundle of consumers for manufactured exports whose politicians usually, by default, defer to Washington. The EU has ambitions of “strategic autonomy” but the process is slow and expensive. It means evolution from soft power – rivalling the US and China in economic heft as a single market whose regulations set global standards – to something a lot harder. European electorates may despise Trump and fear Putin, but they are not all comfortable with the choices that follow if the remedy is a shift in budget priorities to higher defence spending.

A lot of European politics in recent years has been driven with a longing eye on the rear view mirror, wondering if there is a way back to the old world of open trade, respect for international law, a White House that wouldn’t abet the Kremlin in an imperial land grab. But there is growing recognition that Europe’s future cannot resemble its recent past.

The UK is part of that story, and Andy Burnham has understood the implications. In a speech on Monday , the prime minister expanded his criticism of Brexit from the economic to the geopolitical arena. It was, he said, “the first domino to fall” in a pattern of global fragmentation. It introduced a schism in European alliances that was “exactly what our enemies wanted”. Burnham’s audit of the costs in forfeited trade was familiar enough, but he moved the argument up a gear by noting that withdrawal from the top table of European decision-making has cost Britain power and influence in the world. That is something continuity Brexiters cannot compute.

after newsletter promotion

As Burnham finds his pro-European voice, the old Eurosceptic myth-making industrial complex is grinding back into motion. Newspapers have published tenuous stories about the cost of restored alignment with Brussels and hypothetical migrant influxes. Veterans of the leave campaign are limbering up for a dismal dance around the 2016 totem pole. It is rotten from exposure to a decade of international storms.

Britain is a regional power that undervalued the amplifying effect of EU membership. The benefits of being in the club felt enough like great-power status to fool Eurosceptics into thinking they could go it alone. They cling to that delusion. Kemi Badenoch has written about Britain having “latent great power attributes”. She doesn’t have a theory of how those dormant traits will be awoken in a world carved into continental blocs.

Burnham’s plan is hardly precise, but at least he starts with facts: Britain is a European country; Europe will be safer and richer if it pools its resources; the UK should not want to be on the margin.

A summit where Xi, Putin and Trump claim to be deciding the fate of the world may not yield much in the way of concrete deals, but it still contains a warning to European democracies. And a choice. One option is to boost leverage through closer continental cooperation. The alternative is flight into fantasies of immaculate national sovereignty and resurrected historical grandeur. One of those routes is a way for Europe to grow autonomy, security and prosperity in the 21st century. The other is the path of bitter self-defeat modelled by Brexit .

stories.body:
Can the newly listed AI company really be worth $2tn? Anyone who remembers the late 1990s has good reason to ask

Business live – latest updates

R oll up, roll up, who wants to buy shares in a company whose technology “could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, as the prospectus had it? Virtually everybody, as it turned out. Anthropic flew out of the blocks on its first day as a listed company .

From the point of view of the promoters, the result was as good as it gets. The final pricing for the shares at $83 apiece was meaningfully higher than the indicated range of $70 to $78, but still left room for a big initial “pop”. There were positive vibes all round – especially for the battalion of investment banks collecting $550m of underwriting fees .

And, to be fair, it wasn’t nailed-on that the show would go so swimmingly. There was a late risk that investor sentiment towards the AI universe could be jinxed – or Jensened – by the soap opera at Nvidia . More generally, there was a worry that the AI bubble, if that’s what it is, could burst when somebody tried to unload too much stock on the stock market in one go.

Anthropic, though, has set records by raising $107bn. It is an extraordinary sum, especially for a business founded five years ago. At the listing price, Anthropic was valued at $1.5tn. When shares began trading at £111.50, its market capitalisation was up to $2tn. Only 14 months ago, it raised money at a valuation of a “mere” $183bn .

The feat, though, is not wholly inexplicable. Some $26bn of the listing proceeds were virtually in the bag, thanks to the cornerstone placement to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC. That assembly of AI and AI-adjacent names fed worries about the industry’s circular financing.

But, on the other hand, every fund manager knew he or she would be betting against the crowd by saying no. Momentum can carry a stock a long way, even before the index funds and index-hugging funds are obliged to buy (Nasdaq entry will be quick; the S&P 500 will take at least a year).

Take a step back, though, and ask whether Anthropic – loss-making and with projected revenues in 2026 of $50bn-ish – can possibly be worth $1.5tn-plus.

The short, and unhelpful, answer is that virtually any valuation could be made to sound plausible if you believe, first, that AI is a generational technology that will be adopted at never-seen-before speed and, second, that “frontier” pioneering firms, of which Anthropic is the leader, will capture an outsized slice of the commercial value for years and years.

Consider the assumptions behind that thesis, however. Can Anthropic really improve from $50bn-ish of revenue this year to $600bn in 2030, which is roughly what tech analysts have pencilled in? Given the current rate of growth, perhaps it can. But sustaining the pace, or something like it, for another 16 quarters simply won’t be straightforward or mechanical.

What is the real level of demand from corporate users for frontier models? Nobody doubts that AI adoption is still in the early stage, but does everybody need the finest product from Anthropic’s Claude suite? Already executives grumble that their IT budgets are finite and that nine-month-old versions, or cheaper “open weight” models from rivals, do the job for basic work. Lasting pricing power in AI is simply unclear. “Commoditisation risk”, in the jargon, could be the next year’s valuation debate.

Then there is the investment bill to make it all happen – $900bn of spending commitments were detailed in the prospectus for computing power and infrastructure. The listing proceeds help, as does the visibility and credibility that comes with being on a public market. But debt, not just equity, will be a crucial part of this story.

after newsletter promotion

“Obviously, at some point in the future we’re hoping to be investment grade,” said co-founder Dario Amodei as trading in the shares started. You bet: the price at which Anthropic borrows matters fundamentally.

Away from the party atmosphere, the European Central Bank has its eye on financial stability in the eurozone. This week, it issued one of those fuddy-duddy reminders about how much capital is being bet on the AI revolution , and how little transparency there is around the funding of hyperscalers and other suppliers to the boom.

“Big tech firms are estimated to have total off-balance-sheet commitments of more than $4tn as of the second quarter of 2026,” its report said, warning of “historical parallels with the dotcom and sub-prime bubbles”.

It is not the only one to see warning signs. Anthropic is an astonishingly successful company already and is plainly at the forefront of a significant technological shift. But it has been listed in an environment that looks – to most of us who remember the late 1990s and the subsequent bust – to have bubbly characteristics. AI technology, like the internet, is gamechanging. But it doesn’t mean today’s share prices are right.

Increase in October piles pressure on households as Iran war pushes up oil cost and rattles global economy

Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to rise by 26% to £2,166 from January

Inflation in the UK rose to 3.6% in October after petrol prices increased and diesel hit a record high amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East.

Figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) show the headline rate of inflation as measured by the consumer prices index rose from 3.5% in September and was in line with City economists’ forecasts.

As households brace for the colder winter months with household gas and electricity costs soaring, the latest figures push the headline inflation rate to the highest level in a year.

In a reading underscoring the pressure on the Bank of England to raise interest rates, the ONS said fuel prices were the major contributor. Annual costs of raw materials and goods leaving factories also continued to climb, driven by rising energy and crude oil prices amid the Iran war.

Fuel prices for motorists rose at an annual rate of 33.2%, the largest increase since July 2022 after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sparked a global surge in energy prices.

The average price of petrol rose by 5.2p a litre between September and October to reach 174.7p a litre, the highest level in four years. Diesel prices rose by 7p a litre to 199.5p a litre, the highest price on records dating back to 1996.

Andy Burnham’s government has pledged to offer support for households grappling with a fresh cost of living squeeze as the stop-start Iran conflict rattles the global economy and drives up inflation worldwide.

At the budget last month the chancellor, John Healey, announced plans for a £100 winter handout for 20m households to cushion the blow from the global economic storm.

The latest inflation figures took into account a 4% increase in the Ofgem energy price cap from the start of October.

A forecast from the consultancy Cornwall Insight on Wednesday predicted a 26% jump in energy bills in Great Britain from January to the equivalent of £2,166 a year for a typical household.

Economic forecasters predict a further rise in inflation, with the Bank of England anticipating a peak of close to 5% next year.

Earlier this month, Threadneedle Street raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4% and warned further increases in the cost of borrowing might be required to combat inflationary pressures unleashed by the Iran war.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, said the longer the conflict continued the more likely it was that rate increases would be needed, despite a recent drop in global energy prices since the US midterm elections.

Speaking at a conference in London on Tuesday, Bailey said inflation was “probably going to be a bit less” than the 5% forecast made by the Bank earlier this month.

after newsletter promotion

However, he said that if the war pushed energy prices higher, the “more likely persistent inflationary effects will take hold and the higher the level of interest rates will need to be”.

Financial markets anticipate at least two quarter-point increases before the end of next year. Analysts said the Bank could raise borrowing costs from as early as next month.

Core inflation – which excludes volatile energy, food, alcohol and tobacco prices – was unchanged at 2.8%, matching economists’ forecasts. Services inflation, which the Bank has been monitoring closely for evidence of domestic inflationary pressures becoming entrenched, also held steady at 3.7%, slightly below City predictions for a rate of 3.8%.

Air fares rose by 1.8% between September and October amid an increase in long-haul ticket prices – offset by a downward effect from European flights. Prices for alcohol and tobacco also rose, by 4.5%, influenced by the timing of an increase in tobacco duty at the start of the month.

Food prices rose at the slowest rate since September 2021, at 0.9%, down from 1.3% in September.

Emma Reynolds, the chief secretary to the Treasury, said: “The conflict in the Middle East and Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine have pushed up costs around the world.

“The household energy payment, announced in our budget, is providing £100 directly into 20 million bank accounts in January, which will help to give families breathing space now.

“The budget also started the long-term action needed to get energy costs down for good, including an end to levies on household bills, scrapping standing charges and ensuring Britain is better protected from global shocks in the future.”
